title: Path traversal in static data file loader
description: `loadStaticData` directly incorporates its exported `file` argument into a filesystem path without validating it against an allowlist or preventing `..` path traversal. A caller outside this file can supply values such as `../../some-directory/secret`, causing the resolved path to escape `./data/static/` and read any reachable file whose name ends in `.yml`; the contents are then parsed and returned to the caller. This can expose configuration, credentials, or other sensitive YAML files readable by the application process.

trace.description: Exported function `loadStaticData(file)` receives the filename from a caller outside this file; the parameter is not constrained to known static-data names.

The untrusted `file` value is concatenated into a filesystem path before resolution. No allowlist, basename check, or traversal rejection is applied, so `..` segments can escape the intended static-data directory.
`readFile` opens the resolved attacker-influenced path and returns its contents after YAML parsing, enabling unauthorized local file disclosure when a reachable YAML file is selected.

title: Unvalidated snippet key enables HTTP path manipulation
description: The service interpolates the caller-provided `key` directly into an HTTP URL without encoding or constraining it to a snippet identifier. A caller outside this file can supply path separators and traversal segments (for example, `../api/Users`) or query syntax, causing the browser to request a different path than the intended `/snippets/<key>` endpoint. If the host server normalizes such paths, this can expose or invoke unrelated same-origin API resources with the user's browser credentials, or bypass the intended snippet-resource boundary.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies the `key` argument to the exported service method; the argument is accepted without an allow-list or identifier validation.
The untrusted key is concatenated into the request URL, preserving attacker-controlled path and query syntax instead of encoding it as a single path segment.

HttpClient issues the manipulated URL to the configured host. Path traversal or path injection can redirect the request to another same-origin resource, potentially returning unauthorized data or triggering an unintended API operation under the user's credentials.

title: Malformed localStorage data causes conversation service denial of service
description: The service treats the client-controlled localStorage value as valid JSON and as an array without any error handling or structural validation. A same-origin attacker, compromised browser extension, or corrupted storage entry can replace `juiceshop_chat_conversations` with malformed JSON or valid non-array JSON. Any caller of `getAll()` then throws from `JSON.parse()` or `conversations.sort()`, preventing conversation loading and potentially breaking UI flows that depend on this service. The caller is outside this file, but `getAll()` is an exported service method receiving storage data from outside the service.

trace.description: Caller outside this file invokes the exported `getAll()` method; the method reads the attacker-influenced browser storage entry.
The raw localStorage value is parsed directly with `JSON.parse()` and is not wrapped in error handling or checked to be an array of `StoredConversation` records.

The parsed value is unconditionally used as an array and sorted. Malformed JSON throws at parsing, while a valid object or other non-array value throws at `.sort()`, causing callers to fail instead of recovering or clearing invalid state.

title: Guest-basket merge proceeds with caller-controlled target basket after authorization failure
description: The exported merge workflow accepts an arbitrary basket identifier from its caller and uses it to read and then write basket data. If the initial basket lookup fails—including because the basket is unauthorized or nonexistent—the catch handler replaces the result with an empty basket and continues. It subsequently submits a create request containing the caller-controlled `BasketId` (and may submit updates based on returned item identifiers). If the backend does not independently enforce basket ownership on the POST/PUT endpoints, an authenticated attacker can invoke this method with another user's basket ID and add or modify items in that basket. The client-side error fallback also masks authorization failures and deliberately proceeds with a mutation rather than aborting.

trace.description: Entrypoint: `mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket` is callable by a caller outside this file and accepts `targetBasketId` without validating that it belongs to the current user.
The supplied basket ID is used in an authenticated basket lookup. The caller can substitute an arbitrary basket identifier.
Any lookup error is converted into an empty basket, so an authorization or existence failure does not stop the subsequent mutation workflow.

The workflow creates merge requests using the attacker-selected `targetBasketId` as the `BasketId` property. This sends a cross-basket mutation to the backend instead of aborting when the target could not be authorized.

title: Unbounded chat request and response buffering can exhaust client memory
description: The chat stream has no client-side bounds on request size, response duration, or buffered chunks. `streamMessages` accepts an arbitrarily large messages array and submits it directly, while each streamed response chunk is appended to an ever-growing `chunks` array. The HTTP subscription is not retained or cancelled when the async generator consumer stops, so abandoning the generator leaves the request active and causes all subsequent output to accumulate in memory. A user-controlled prompt that induces a very large or long-lived model response, or simply navigating away while a response continues, can exhaust browser memory and degrade or crash the client.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies an unrestricted `messages` array to the exported async generator; there are no size, count, or content-length limits at this boundary.
The caller-provided messages are serialized into a POST request without a client-side size limit, timeout, cancellation handle, or other resource control.

Every streamed delta is converted into a chunk and appended to `chunks`; the array is never trimmed after chunks are yielded, so memory usage grows with the entire response. The subscription is also not exposed for cancellation if the generator consumer abandons iteration.

The generator continues waiting for and yielding data until the remote stream ends, while accumulated chunks and the active subscription remain live. An unbounded or long-lived response therefore provides a direct client-side memory and availability sink.

title: Caller-controlled review author identity
description: The service sends the caller-supplied `author` field directly to the review API. Because the client can be modified or the API can be called directly, an attacker can submit a review while claiming another username or identity unless the server independently derives and authorizes the author from the authenticated session. This undermines review attribution and can enable impersonation or fraudulent content attribution.

trace.description: The exported `create` method receives a review object containing an externally supplied `author` field; its caller is outside this file and may provide attacker-controlled values.
The supplied review object, including `author`, is forwarded unchanged as the HTTP request body for the product review operation.

The HTTP PUT request persists or processes the caller-controlled `author` property at `/rest/products/{id}/reviews`. If the server trusts this field rather than deriving the identity from authentication, an attacker can impersonate another reviewer.

title: Client-controlled X-User-Email header can enable user impersonation
description: The interceptor copies the browser-controlled `localStorage.email` value into an `X-User-Email` request header. Any script running in the origin, browser extension, or user-controlled client can modify this value before making a request. If backend authorization or resource ownership logic consumes this header as the caller identity instead of deriving identity solely from the verified bearer token/session, an attacker can impersonate another user by setting the value to that user's email and access or modify their resources. Client-provided identity headers are not an authorization control and must not be trusted for authentication or ownership decisions.

trace.description: The Angular HTTP interceptor receives every outgoing request from callers outside this file; the caller and attacker-facing route are outside the inspected file.

Before forwarding the request, the interceptor reads the mutable browser `localStorage.email` value and places it in the `X-User-Email` header without binding it to the authenticated token or validating it against a trusted server-side identity.

The request is forwarded with an attacker-controlled identity assertion in `X-User-Email`. Any server endpoint that uses this header for identity, ownership, or authorization decisions can be reached with another user's email, enabling impersonation and unauthorized object access or modification.

title: Unencoded email enables query-parameter injection
description: The `findBy` method interpolates the caller-supplied email directly into the query string without URL encoding. A caller can supply values containing `&`, `=`, or additional query syntax, causing the generated request to contain attacker-controlled parameters beyond the intended `email` parameter. Depending on server-side query parsing, this enables parameter pollution or manipulation of the security-question lookup request, potentially changing which account is queried or altering endpoint behavior.

trace.description: The exported `findBy(email)` method receives caller-controlled email data; the caller and its input validation are outside this file.
The email value is concatenated directly into a URL after `email=` without `encodeURIComponent` or equivalent query-parameter serialization.
Angular HttpClient issues the constructed request to the security-question endpoint, allowing injected query syntax in `email` to reach the backend request parser.

title: Untrusted feedback comments bypass Angular sanitization and enable stored XSS
description: Feedback comments received from the feedback service are embedded directly into an HTML string and then explicitly marked as trusted with Angular's DomSanitizer bypass API. An attacker who can submit or control a feedback comment can inject HTML such as an element with an event handler (for example, an payload); the trusted value is subsequently supplied to the gallery for rendering, bypassing Angular's normal sanitization and enabling stored client-side XSS for visitors to the About page.

trace.description: The component receives the feedback collection from feedbackService.find(). The caller and the attacker-facing feedback submission path are outside this file.

Each feedback.comment value is interpolated into a dynamically constructed HTML fragment without validation or sanitization. The value is placed inside a

element, but an attacker can close that element and inject additional HTML.

The dynamically constructed fragment is passed to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(), explicitly disabling Angular's HTML sanitization. The resulting trusted HTML is then supplied as gallery image arguments and rendered by the gallery component, allowing injected markup and event-handler payloads to execute in visitors' browsers.

title: Unbounded loading of orders, stock, and products into browser memory
description: The component performs unbounded client-side retrieval of accounting data. `loadOrders()` calls `orderHistoryService.getAll()` and stores every returned order in an array before constructing a `MatTableDataSource`; `loadQuantity()` similarly retrieves all stock records. No page size, server-side pagination, result cap, or cancellation is applied in this file. An attacker who can trigger the accounting component repeatedly, or an account with access to this view in an environment containing a large number of orders/products, can cause the browser to download and retain an arbitrarily large response, consuming client memory and CPU and potentially degrading service through repeated large requests. The same pattern also appears in the product search with an empty query, which may return the complete product catalog.

trace.description: The Angular lifecycle hook, invoked by the framework when this component is rendered (caller is outside this file), triggers all three accounting data loads without accepting or enforcing a page size.

`loadQuantity()` requests the complete stock collection through `quantityService.getAll()`, while `loadProducts()` searches with an empty string and `loadOrders()` requests the complete order collection through `orderHistoryService.getAll()`; no pagination or response limit is supplied.

The complete order response is copied into `orderData` and then used to construct a client-side `MatTableDataSource`; equivalent unbounded client-side storage occurs for stock and products. This is the resource-consumption sink because response size and in-memory table size are not bounded.

title: Password change sends credentials in a GET URL
description: The test explicitly exercises a password-change operation as a GET request whose query string contains the current and new passwords. Query parameters are commonly stored in browser history, reverse-proxy/web-server access logs, monitoring systems, referrer data, and other intermediaries, allowing credential disclosure even when the connection is otherwise encrypted. The test codifies and validates this unsafe transport pattern in UserService rather than requiring a POST body.

trace.description: The test invokes UserService.changePassword with current and new password values; the service implementation is outside this file, but this test is the caller-facing evidence of the request contract.
The test expects the request URL to include current, new, and repeat password values as query parameters.

The test requires the request method to be GET, confirming that password material is placed in a URL rather than sent in a POST/PATCH body. Any URL logging or history capture can expose the passwords.

title: OAuth access token is transmitted in a URL query parameter
description: The OAuth login test requires UserService to send an access token in the URL query string. Access tokens in URLs can leak through browser history, proxy/server access logs, telemetry, and referrer propagation. Although this file uses HttpTestingController and does not make a real external request itself, it codifies the insecure token transport contract for the service.

trace.description: The test invokes UserService.oauthLogin with an access-token value; the service implementation is outside this file, but this test supplies the token to that request path.
The expected request URL includes the supplied access token as the access_token query parameter.
The test requires a GET request to the token-bearing URL, validating a transport pattern that can expose the token to URL logging and history mechanisms.

title: Password-change credentials exposed in GET URL
description: The password-change operation transmits the current password, new password, and repeat password as URL query parameters in a GET request. URLs are commonly retained in browser history, proxy/web-server logs, monitoring systems, and other intermediary records, exposing credentials to parties that can access those records. The values are also concatenated without URL encoding, so password characters such as '&' or '#' can alter the request and cause incorrect or partial credential transmission. An attacker who obtains URL logs or browser history can recover the submitted passwords.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies the current, new, and repeated passwords to the exported changePassword method.
The password fields are directly interpolated into a URL query string without URL encoding.
HttpClient performs a GET request containing all password values in the request URL, making them available to URL history and intermediary/request logging.

title: OAuth bearer token exposed in URL query string
description: The OAuth access token is placed directly in the query string of an outbound userinfo request. Although the destination uses HTTPS, bearer tokens in URLs can be captured by browser history, network/proxy/server access logs, telemetry, or referrer-related handling. Anyone obtaining the URL can replay the token until it expires or is revoked, gaining access to the associated Google identity information.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies an OAuth access token to the exported oauthLogin method.
The token is concatenated into the userinfo URL as the access_token query parameter.
HttpClient sends the bearer token as part of the request URL, where it may be retained or disclosed by URL and request logging infrastructure and later replayed.

title: Authentication state set before login succeeds
description: login() publishes isLoggedIn=true before the authentication request has succeeded. Subscribers can therefore observe an authenticated state immediately for invalid credentials, network failures, or rejected login responses. If route guards or UI components rely on this service state for access decisions, an unauthenticated user can reach authenticated client-side functionality by initiating a failed login; this state also remains incorrect unless another component explicitly resets it.

trace.description: The caller outside this file invokes login with attacker-controlled login parameters.
The service immediately emits an authenticated state before subscribing to or receiving the server's authentication result.
The login request is only initiated after the optimistic authenticated-state emission, so failed authentication can still expose true to consumers of getLoggedInState().

title: Login guard accepts arbitrary token-like local-storage values
description: The authentication guard is tested as accepting any non-empty local-storage value as proof of authentication: the test stores the literal malformed value `TOKEN` and expects `canActivate()` to return true. If the production guard implements this contract, an attacker who can write to browser storage can bypass the client-side login gate with an arbitrary string rather than a validated, non-expired, cryptographically verified token. Client-side guards are not a substitute for server-side authorization, but this test establishes an insecure authentication requirement and fails to require token validation on the access-control path.

trace.description: The test framework invokes the LoginGuard authentication behavior; the production caller and implementation are outside this file.
The test supplies the arbitrary, non-JWT string `TOKEN` directly through the browser's local storage token slot, without a signature, expiration, or structural validity check.
The test asserts that the guard grants access solely because the token slot is non-empty, establishing acceptance of an unvalidated authentication credential.

title: Authentication guard accepts any localStorage token value
description: The route guard treats the mere presence of a non-empty value in client-controlled localStorage as proof that the user is authenticated. An attacker can set an arbitrary value such as `localStorage.setItem('token', 'attacker-controlled')` and satisfy any route protected only by LoginGuard. This bypasses client-side access restrictions; any sensitive operation whose protection relies on this guard may become reachable, although server-side authorization is not visible in this file.

trace.description: Angular invokes canActivate from outside this file during navigation; the caller supplies no trusted authentication result to this guard.
The guard reads a token directly from attacker-modifiable browser localStorage and checks only whether a value exists; it does not validate token structure, signature, expiry, or issuer.
Any non-empty localStorage value causes the guard to return true, allowing navigation to the protected route.

title: Client-side role authorization trusts an unsigned JWT payload
description: Admin and accounting authorization decisions are based on fields from a JWT that is only decoded in the browser. `jwtDecode` parses the payload but does not verify the token's cryptographic signature. Because the token is read from client-controlled localStorage, an attacker can modify or replace it with a token whose decoded role is `admin` or `accounting`, causing the corresponding client-side guard to allow navigation. This is a broken client-side privilege check and must not be relied upon for server authorization.

trace.description: Angular invokes AdminGuard.canActivate from outside this file when an administrator-only route is navigated to.
AdminGuard obtains the token payload through LoginGuard.tokenDecode, with the token ultimately sourced from browser localStorage.
The token is passed to jwtDecode, which decodes the payload but performs no signature or issuer verification; malformed-token errors are only logged.
The guard authorizes the route solely by comparing the untrusted decoded role field to roles.admin. A locally modified payload containing the admin role makes this check succeed.

title: Route-controlled address ID is used without an ownership check
description: The component treats the `addressId` route parameter as sufficient authority to read and modify an address. A caller outside this file can navigate to an arbitrary address ID; the component passes that ID directly to `AddressService.getById()` and later to `AddressService.put()` without any ownership or authorization check. If the corresponding API does not independently enforce that the authenticated user owns the address, User A can view and overwrite User B's address by substituting B's identifier in the route. Client-side routing must not be relied upon as an authorization control.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies route state through Angular's `ActivatedRoute`; this component subscribes to the route parameter map.
The component accepts the externally controlled `addressId` parameter and switches into edit mode without validating that the ID belongs to the current user.
The arbitrary route ID is passed directly to the address lookup service, allowing a user who can obtain another address ID to request that address.

When saving in edit mode, the same unverified route ID and the client-constructed address object are passed to the update service. No per-resource ownership or authorization check occurs in this component before the mutation.

The update operation is issued for the caller-selected address ID. Without equivalent server-side authorization, this is an IDOR/BOLA mutation allowing unauthorized modification of another user's address.

title: Sensitive account routes lack authentication guards
description: Several sensitive authenticated workflows are reachable through Angular routes without any LoginGuard. In particular, the privacy/security parent route exposes password-change, two-factor-authentication, data-export, and last-login-IP pages, while saved payment methods and order history are also directly routable. An unauthenticated user can navigate directly to these paths and instantiate the associated components instead of being redirected to login. Because this file provides no authentication gate for these sensitive client-side entrypoints, the UI and any component-side operations are exposed unless every downstream component and API independently compensates for the missing route control.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the Angular router receives attacker-controlled navigation URLs and matches them against the route table.

The route table exposes `saved-payment-methods`, `order-history`, and `privacy-security` without `canActivate: [LoginGuard]`; the privacy/security route also nests sensitive child pages without a guard on the parent or children.

Unauthenticated navigation reaches `SavedPaymentMethodsComponent`, `OrderHistoryComponent`, and the privacy/security child components, including `ChangePasswordComponent`, `TwoFactorAuthComponent`, `DataExportComponent`, and `LastLoginIpComponent`, without a route-level authentication check.

title: OAuth bearer token is propagated directly from the URL fragment
description: The OAuth route accepts an access token delivered in the browser URL fragment and copies the entire fragment into Angular route data. This leaves the bearer token resident in `window.location.href` and propagates it to `OAuthComponent`, increasing exposure through browser history, screenshots, browser extensions, injected scripts, and client-side diagnostics. The route performs no visible token validation, expiry enforcement, or secure exchange before handing the value to the component. A stolen token can permit access to the OAuth-protected account for its validity period, depending on provider scope and token lifetime.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the browser invokes the custom matcher during navigation while the current URL may contain an OAuth `#access_token` fragment.
`oauthMatcher` authorizes the route solely when `window.location.href` contains `#access_token=`, without validating the token, its issuer, signature, audience, or expiry in this file.

The matching route copies the complete substring beginning at `#` from `window.location.href` into route data and supplies it to `OAuthComponent`, making the bearer credential directly available to client-side code as URL-derived data.

title: Privileged password policy is advisory and does not block the password change
description: The component detects that a support account's new password fails the stronger privileged-account policy, but only writes a client-console warning and continues to submit the password change. The policy is therefore advisory and can be bypassed simply by invoking the normal change-password action with a weak password (and client-side state such as localStorage is not a suitable enforcement boundary). If this policy is intended to protect privileged support accounts, the backend must reject the transition rather than allowing the request to proceed after the warning. This can result in privileged accounts being assigned passwords that do not meet the stated policy.

trace.description: The UI invokes changePassword; the caller and attacker-facing interaction are outside this file.
For an email matching support@..., the component checks whether the new password satisfies the stronger 12–30 character, mixed-character privileged-account policy.
When the policy check fails, the component only emits console.error and does not return, invalidate the form, or otherwise prevent the operation.
The component unconditionally sends the current, new, and repeated passwords to UserService.changePassword, allowing the weak privileged password to be submitted.

title: Sensitive chatbot messages exposed through URL query parameters
description: The component places the complete user-supplied chat message into the `initialMessage` query parameter. This causes potentially sensitive chat content, including credentials, personal data, or proprietary information voluntarily entered into the chatbot, to be exposed in the browser's URL, history, copied links, referrer headers, and upstream access/proxy logs. An attacker who can access browser history, shared URLs, referrer data, or infrastructure logs can recover the message. Sensitive message content should be transferred through application state or a request body rather than a URL query parameter.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the component receives an arbitrary chat message through the `message` handler argument.
The received message is forwarded unchanged as the `initialMessage` query parameter during router navigation.
Angular navigation updates the browser URL with the query parameter, making the full message available to URL/history/referrer and HTTP access-log mechanisms.

title: Continuation token stored without Secure or SameSite protections
description: A server-returned continuation code is stored as a long-lived browser cookie without explicit transport or cross-site protections. The exported helper receives the challenge result from a caller outside this file, requests a continuation code when the result is true, and writes that code with only a one-year expiration. Because Secure and SameSite are not configured, the token can be exposed over an HTTP deployment and may be sent in cross-site requests; anyone who obtains it may be able to continue the associated challenge workflow as the victim. The one-year lifetime further increases the replay window.

trace.description: The exported helper receives the verdict and service dependencies from a caller outside this file; an attacker-controlled or otherwise manipulated client-side verdict can enter this flow, although the server-side reachability is outside the reviewed file.
When the verdict is true, the helper invokes the challenge continuation API and consumes its returned continuation code.
The returned code is retained for one year and passed directly to the cookie service. The options specify only expiration, with no explicit Secure or SameSite attributes.

title: Client-controlled address identifier used without an ownership check
description: The component uses the browser-controlled `sessionStorage` value `addressId` as the sole identifier supplied to `AddressService.getById()`. There is no ownership or authorization check in this component before the address is retrieved and assigned for use in the checkout flow. A user can alter `sessionStorage.addressId` to another address identifier; if the corresponding service/API does not independently scope the lookup to the authenticated user, this enables access to another user's address and potentially use of that address during checkout. Client-side storage must not be treated as an authorization boundary.

trace.description: The component receives the target address identifier from attacker-modifiable browser session storage; the caller and any code that writes this value are outside this file.

The raw `addressId` value is passed directly to `AddressService.getById()` without validation, binding it to the authenticated user, or checking that the selected address belongs to the current account.

`getById()` is invoked as the resource lookup and its response is accepted into `this.address` for the checkout flow. No per-resource authorization check is visible between the attacker-controlled identifier and use of the returned address; an attacker can substitute another user's address ID and obtain/use it if the backend does not enforce ownership.

title: Untrusted JWT claim passed through Angular HTML sanitizer bypass
description: The component reads a JWT directly from attacker-modifiable browser storage, decodes its payload without signature verification, and embeds the `lastLoginIp` claim into HTML passed through Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`. If the claim contains markup such as an event-handler payload, the resulting trusted HTML can execute when the component template renders it via an HTML sink (for example, `[innerHTML]`). The explicit sanitizer bypass removes Angular's normal XSS protection, and no validation or sanitization is applied to the claim.

trace.description: Entrypoint: this component receives external client-side data by reading the `token` value from `localStorage`; the caller and source of that storage value are outside this file, and same-origin script or token-poisoning paths can influence it.
The token is decoded solely as a JWT payload with `jwtDecode`; this operation does not verify the token signature. The code then reads the unvalidated `payload.data.lastLoginIp` value.
The untrusted claim is copied into `lastLoginIp` after being interpolated into an HTML string; there is no input validation or sanitization of the claim.
Sink: `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` explicitly marks attacker-influenced HTML as safe, allowing markup and event-handler/script-capable payloads to reach the component's HTML rendering sink.

title: Password-recovery flow enables account enumeration
description: The password-recovery UI uses a caller-supplied email address to query whether a user exists and then exposes the returned security question. An unauthenticated attacker can submit candidate email addresses and distinguish registered accounts from nonexistent ones based on whether the response is truthy and the controls are enabled. For registered accounts, the security question is also revealed, assisting targeted password-reset attacks. The caller/template and backend route are outside this file, but this component clearly performs and exposes the result of the lookup.

trace.description: The email form control receives attacker-controlled input from the forgot-password page; the page/template caller is outside this file.
When an email value is present, the component passes it directly to the security-question lookup service.
The component makes the lookup request using the supplied email address.
The response is treated as an existence signal: a truthy security-question response enables the reset controls, while a falsey response disables them.

For an existing account, the returned security question is assigned to component state and is subsequently rendered by the forgot-password template, exposing account existence and the question to the requester.

title: Password-recovery lookup lacks an effective rate-limit control
description: The component exposes a public password-recovery lookup operation with only a one-second client-side debounce. There is no server-enforced rate-limit or lockout control in this code path. An attacker can bypass the browser debounce by issuing requests directly to the service endpoint or by using multiple clients, repeatedly causing security-question lookups and consuming backend request, connection, and database resources. Any infrastructure-level throttling would need to be verified elsewhere.

trace.description: The forgot-password page invokes this handler in response to attacker-controlled email-entry activity; the template/event caller is outside this file.
The component applies only a local one-second timer, which throttles a single browser instance but provides no protection against direct or distributed requests.
After the timer expires, the component issues a security-question lookup for the supplied email address.

title: Hardcoded testing credentials exposed in the client bundle
description: The login component contains a hardcoded username and plaintext password for a testing account. Because these are public component properties, they are included in the client-side application bundle and can be recovered by any user who downloads or inspects the frontend. An attacker can use the disclosed credentials to authenticate as the testing account, potentially gaining access to its data and functionality. Credentials should not be embedded in client-delivered source, even when intended only for testing.

trace.description: Angular instantiates LoginComponent as part of the login route; the framework caller and frontend bundle serving this component are outside this file.
The component declares the testing username as a public property, making it available to the component template and client-side bundle.

The corresponding plaintext testing password is hardcoded in the browser-delivered source. Anyone can inspect the JavaScript bundle and use this username/password pair against the login flow, resulting in unauthorized authentication as the testing account.

title: Client-controlled feedback user identity
description: The component treats the client-side `userIdControl` value as the authoritative identity for a feedback submission. Although it is initially populated from `whoAmI`, the control is public and client state can be modified through browser developer tools or by intercepting the request. `save()` then copies that mutable value into `feedback.UserId` and submits it. If the feedback API persists the supplied `UserId` rather than deriving the submitter from the authenticated session, an attacker can attribute feedback to another user or otherwise forge ownership metadata. Client-side controls are not an authorization boundary; the server must ignore caller-supplied identity fields and derive the user from authentication.

trace.description: The component receives the authenticated user identity from the `whoAmI` service; the service and its caller are outside this file.
The returned user ID is copied into the mutable `userIdControl` form control.
The same client-derived value is stored in the feedback object as `UserId`, making identity attribution part of the client-submitted object.
On submission, the component reads the current value of the client-controlled form control. A user can alter this value before submission.
The feedback object, including the caller-controlled `UserId` property, is sent to the feedback API. The API must derive identity server-side rather than trusting this field.

title: Unsanitized exported data written into a same-origin document
description: The component writes the `userData` field from the data-export API response directly into a newly opened document using `document.write`, without escaping or sanitizing it. The exported data can contain attacker-controlled stored values (for example, profile or other user-submitted fields). When a victim performs a data export, HTML payloads embedded in that data are parsed and can execute in the new same-origin window, enabling stored/reflected client-side XSS against the victim's session and origin.

trace.description: The component receives the data-export API response; the caller and server-side response construction are outside this file. The response is accepted in the subscription callback without establishing that `userData` is safe HTML.
The response's `userData` field is copied directly to component state, preserving any HTML-bearing or attacker-controlled content returned by the API.

The untrusted `userData` value is passed to `document.write` in a newly opened same-origin window. The browser parses the value as HTML, so injected markup such as event-handler attributes or script-capable HTML can execute without an intervening sanitizer or escaping step.

title: OAuth users receive deterministic reversible passwords derived from email addresses
description: The OAuth account-creation flow is verified to generate the user's password as a reversible transformation of the email address: the email is reversed and Base64-encoded. Base64 is not encryption or password hashing, and the email is generally public or guessable. An attacker who knows an OAuth user's email can deterministically derive the password and potentially authenticate through the regular login flow, as demonstrated by the subsequent fallback login expectation.

trace.description: The OAuth login result supplies an email address to the component; the caller and production OAuth provider are outside this test file, while this test models the externally received identity data.
The component's OAuth initialization is executed with the supplied email, causing the account-creation workflow to process that identity.

The test asserts that the component saves a new account using the reversed, Base64-encoded email as both password and password confirmation. This is a deterministic and reversible credential-generation scheme rather than a secret or a password-hashing operation.

title: Order completion page displays orders and addresses for arbitrary route IDs
description: The component treats the route's `id` parameter as sufficient authority to retrieve and display an order. A caller outside this file supplies the route parameter; it is passed directly to `TrackOrderService.find()` without any client-side ownership or authorization check. The returned order's address identifier is then used to fetch and display address data as well. If the backing tracking endpoint does not independently enforce ownership, an authenticated user—or an unauthenticated caller if the endpoint is public—can substitute another customer's order ID and obtain that order and associated address information.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies the attacker-controlled route parameter through Angular's `ActivatedRoute.paramMap` subscription.
The route `id` value is copied directly into `orderId` with no validation or ownership check.
The untrusted order identifier is passed to `TrackOrderService.find()`, initiating retrieval of the selected order without a per-user authorization check in this component.

The response is trusted and its order fields, including `addressId` and products, are copied into component state; the component also uses the returned address ID to request address data without verifying that it belongs to the current user or order viewer.

The fetched address is assigned to component state for rendering, completing the unauthorized data-disclosure path. An attacker can reproduce this by replacing their order ID in the route with another user's order ID.

title: OAuth accounts receive predictable, reversible passwords
description: OAuth-provisioned accounts are assigned a deterministic password derived solely from the user's email: the email is reversed and Base64-encoded. Base64 is reversible and provides no secrecy or key stretching. Anyone who knows an OAuth user's email can compute the same password and attempt password authentication against that account, potentially taking over the account or bypassing the OAuth provider. The generated value is persisted through the user-save flow and reused for login.

trace.description: ngOnInit receives the OAuth profile from the external oauthLogin response and processes it; the caller and OAuth provider are outside this file.
The component derives the account password by reversing profile.email and encoding it with btoa, making the credential fully predictable from a public identity attribute.
The deterministic password is submitted to the user-save operation as the persisted account password and passwordRepeat fields.

title: OAuth callback lacks state validation, enabling login CSRF
description: The OAuth callback accepts an access_token from the redirect parameters and immediately authenticates with it, but this component does not validate an OAuth state value or bind the callback to a login attempt initiated by the same browser session. An attacker can initiate OAuth for an account they control, capture the resulting callback token, and cause a victim to visit the crafted callback URL. The victim's browser then logs into the attacker's account, creating login CSRF and enabling actions the victim believes are being performed on their own account, such as submitting personal data or orders to the attacker-controlled account.

trace.description: ngOnInit handles OAuth callback data; the initiating login context and caller are outside this file.
The callback data is read from the route snapshot and the fragment is parsed into arbitrary key/value parameters without checking an OAuth state value against a session-bound value.
The parser places every supplied key into params and performs no allow-listing or state verification.
The unvalidated access_token is passed directly into oauthLogin, causing the browser to authenticate using whichever token an attacker supplied in the callback URL.

title: Bearer authentication token is exposed to client-side JavaScript
description: After receiving an authentication token, the component stores it in localStorage and also sets it through a JavaScript-accessible cookie. Any script executing in the application's origin can read the localStorage token (and the cookie is not configured here with HttpOnly), allowing token theft and session takeover if an XSS or other same-origin script injection occurs. A browser-managed HttpOnly session cookie or another non-JavaScript-readable token mechanism would avoid exposing the bearer token to page scripts.

trace.description: The login subscription receives an authentication response containing a bearer token from the external user-service call.
The token is placed in a client-managed cookie using CookieService, with no HttpOnly or Secure protections expressed in this code.
The same bearer token is explicitly written to localStorage, where any script running in the origin can read it and replay it for account takeover.

title: Checkout trusts tamperable sessionStorage state
description: The checkout request is constructed entirely from values in browser-controlled sessionStorage. An attacker can modify paymentId, addressId, deliveryMethodId, bid, and couponDetails before invoking placeOrder(), causing the client to submit a different basket or payment/address/delivery selection than the normal workflow establishes. This is an insecure client-trust design: the server-side checkout operation must independently derive or authorize these values and recalculate all financial details, rather than treating the client-supplied identifiers as trusted workflow state. If the backend accepts these identifiers without ownership and state validation, an attacker can place orders against another basket/address/payment method or manipulate checkout data.

trace.description: The component receives checkout state from browser sessionStorage; the caller and any code that populated these values are outside this file, and sessionStorage is directly modifiable by the user.

placeOrder() copies the sessionStorage values directly into orderDetails and also reads the basket ID and couponDetails from sessionStorage without any integrity protection or server-authorized state binding.

The client sends the attacker-modifiable identifiers and coupon data to basketService.checkout(). No client-side authorization, ownership validation, or confirmation that these values belong to the current user or basket occurs before the checkout request.

title: Image validation relies only on attacker-controlled magic-byte prefixes
description: The validator treats a four-byte prefix as proof that the uploaded value is a valid image. Any attacker-controlled file beginning with the PNG signature bytes (`89 50 4e 47`) is accepted at line 42, regardless of whether it contains a valid PNG structure or arbitrary trailing content; analogous checks accept only a small set of JPEG prefixes without parsing the file. If this validator is used as the upload gate, a crafted non-image can pass client-side validation and reach storage or downstream image processing, potentially causing unsafe content delivery or parser-specific attacks. The caller and downstream upload path are outside this file, so exploit impact depends on those components trusting this result.

trace.description: The exported validator receives the Angular control value from a caller outside this file; that value can represent attacker-selected upload data.
The control value is cast to File and read as raw bytes without any structural image parsing or server-side verification shown here.
Only the first four bytes are converted into a header string and compared against a short allowlist of signatures.
A file matching the prefix is marked valid and the validator emits null, allowing downstream upload logic to treat arbitrary trailing content as an acceptable image.

title: Client-controlled basket ID enables unauthorized basket access
description: The component treats the client-controlled `sessionStorage` value `bid` as the authoritative basket identifier. A user can modify this value to another user's basket ID, after which `basketService.find(...)` requests that basket without any ownership or authorization check in this code. If the backend endpoint does not independently scope the lookup to the authenticated user, this enables BOLA: User A can read User B's basket and potentially expose its contents, prices, and quantities. The same trust pattern is also used for basket-item mutation calls in `delete` and `addToQuantity`, enabling unauthorized modification if those backend operations likewise lack server-side ownership checks.

trace.description: `ngOnInit` is invoked by the Angular framework/caller outside this file and calls `load`, which begins loading the authenticated user's basket.
The component only checks whether any token exists, then reads `bid` directly from attacker-modifiable `sessionStorage`; no authenticated-user ownership check is performed on the identifier.

The attacker-controlled basket ID is passed to `basketService.find`, causing the application to request and render the selected basket. Substituting another user's basket ID can retrieve that basket unless the server independently enforces ownership.

title: Client-supplied UserId and AddressId are submitted as authoritative recycle properties
description: The component constructs a recycle request containing caller-controlled resource and identity fields and submits the entire object to the Recycles API. Although `UserId` is initially populated from `whoAmI`, that value exists in the browser and can be changed by the caller before the request is sent. Likewise, `AddressId` is taken from a component handler and is not checked against the authenticated user. If the API accepts these properties, an attacker can create a recycling record under another user's identity or associate it with another user's address. Authorization and ownership must be enforced server-side rather than trusting these client-supplied properties.

trace.description: The `save()` method is called by the component's caller outside this file; it begins processing a recycle submission without establishing server-authoritative ownership or authorization for the target user or address.
The component initializes `recycle.UserId` from the `whoAmI` response, but this value is stored in the client-side mutable `recycle` object and is therefore modifiable by the caller/browser.
`AddressId` is copied from the component's `addressId` state, which is set by the externally invoked `getMessage(id)` handler and is not checked for ownership in this file.

The complete mutable recycle object, including `UserId` and `AddressId`, is submitted to the recycle API. A caller who changes either property can attempt to create a record for another user or use another user's address unless the API rejects or derives these fields server-side.

title: Unvalidated challenge difficulty crashes score-board rendering
description: The component accepts runtime challenge data without validating that `difficulty` is one of the initialized lookup keys. Although the TypeScript type permits difficulty `0`, `INITIAL_SUMMARIES` contains only keys `1` through `6`; an incoming challenge with difficulty `0` or another invalid value makes `summariesLookup[challenge.difficulty]` undefined, and the update at line 58 throws a TypeError. If an attacker can create or modify challenge data consumed by this component, they can cause the score-board view to fail for users, producing client-side denial of service. The same unchecked dynamic lookup also permits prototype-key values if runtime data violates the declared type.

trace.description: The component receives the `allChallenges` array through an Angular input; the caller and the source of these challenge values are outside this file.
The received challenge array is passed directly into `calculateDifficultySummaries` without runtime validation or normalization of each challenge's `difficulty` value.

The code dynamically indexes the fixed lookup object and immediately dereferences the result. For difficulty `0` (allowed by the declared type but absent from `INITIAL_SUMMARIES`) or an attacker-supplied invalid runtime value, the lookup is undefined and this increment throws, interrupting score-board rendering.

title: Untrusted challenge descriptions bypass Angular HTML sanitization
description: Challenge descriptions received from the backend are explicitly marked as trusted HTML with Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, disabling Angular's contextual sanitization. The resulting SafeHtml is intended for an HTML-rendering template binding, so any attacker who can influence a stored challenge description or the API response can inject markup such as an event-handler payload and execute JavaScript in the application's origin. No sanitization or allowlist is applied before the bypass.

trace.description: The component receives challenge records from `ChallengeService.find`; the caller and backend endpoint are outside this file, and the response includes the challenge `description` field.
Each API-provided challenge is copied into the component's rendering model, with its description retained as dynamic content.

The dynamic challenge description is passed directly to `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, explicitly disabling Angular's built-in HTML sanitization. The resulting trusted value is used by the component template for HTML rendering, allowing attacker-supplied markup and event-handler content to execute in the browser.

title: Unsanitized order ID reaches Angular HTML security bypass
description: The component explicitly disables Angular's HTML sanitization with bypassSecurityTrustHtml() and interpolates the API-provided orderId into an HTML string. An attacker who can cause the tracking response to contain HTML payload content (for example through a manipulated or attacker-controlled order identifier/order record) can inject markup such as ``, which Angular will trust and render. This results in client-side XSS in the user's browser.

trace.description: The component receives the tracking identifier from the route query parameter; the caller and attacker-facing route are outside this file. This value controls which tracking response is requested.
The route-derived identifier is passed to TrackOrderService.find(), and the component accepts the returned external API response without validating the orderId field.

The response's orderId is interpolated into an HTML string and passed to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(), explicitly disabling Angular's normal sanitization. The trusted HTML is subsequently rendered by the component template, allowing attacker-supplied tags and event-handler payloads to execute.

title: Post-MFA bearer token stored in JavaScript-accessible storage
description: After successful two-factor verification, the bearer authentication token returned by the service is stored in browser-accessible storage. The token is written to localStorage and also to a client-managed cookie without any visible secure-cookie options. Any script executing in the application's origin, such as through an XSS issue, can read the localStorage token and use it to impersonate the authenticated user, including bypassing the completed MFA step until the token expires or is revoked.

trace.description: The component's verify() handler receives the user-entered MFA token; the caller and UI event are outside this file.
The supplied token is sent to TwoFactorAuthService.verify(), which performs the authentication request; the service implementation is outside this file.
On a successful MFA response, the returned authentication token is written to localStorage, making the bearer credential readable by any JavaScript running in the origin.
The same bearer token is additionally stored through a client-side cookie API with only an expiration value shown; no Secure or other protective cookie attributes are configured at this call site.

title: Raw backend errors exposed through client-side console logging
description: The HTTP error callback writes the complete raw error object to the browser console. Angular HTTP errors can include backend response bodies, stack traces, internal paths, database/API details, or other diagnostic data. Any user who can trigger a failed user-details request can inspect this output in their browser, exposing implementation details that aid further attacks and are not appropriate for production client logging.

trace.description: The component receives the result of an external caller-controlled/user-selected user lookup through the injected UserService; the service call and its backend response originate outside this file.
If the lookup fails, the entire error object is passed unchanged to the error handler rather than being reduced to a safe user-facing message.
The raw error is emitted with console.log, making backend diagnostic content visible to the requesting user through browser developer tools.

title: Client-controlled wallet total is passed to payment flow
description: The wallet amount is taken from a client-controlled form control and written directly to sessionStorage without checking the control's validity or binding the amount to the server-side wallet balance. Client-side Validators only affect UI state and can be bypassed by invoking the handler, modifying the control in developer tools, or editing sessionStorage. The subsequent wallet payment flow can therefore receive an attacker-selected transaction amount, potentially enabling unauthorized wallet credit or payment manipulation if it trusts walletTotal.

trace.description: The component's continue() handler is invoked by the wallet UI/template caller outside this file; it begins the wallet-to-payment transition without enforcing that the requested amount is valid or authorized against the account balance.

The handler reads balanceControl.value, which is supplied by the browser and is subject only to client-side validators declared at line 30; those validators are not an authorization or integrity control.

The attacker-controlled value is persisted as walletTotal in sessionStorage and then consumed by the payment route. Browser users can alter this value directly or bypass the form validation before navigation, allowing the downstream payment flow to process a forged wallet amount if it trusts this client-side state.

title: Unsanitized product descriptions passed through Angular HTML security bypass
description: Product descriptions received from the product service are explicitly marked as trusted HTML without sanitization. If an attacker can create or modify a product description through the product-management API, the payload is carried into the search-result view and rendered as HTML, allowing arbitrary client-side script execution in users' browsers.

trace.description: The component receives the products array from ProductService; the service/API caller is outside this file, so product descriptions must be treated as externally influenced data.
The returned product objects, including each description, are passed to trustProductDescription without validation or sanitization.

bypassSecurityTrustHtml disables Angular's HTML sanitization for each product description. When the resulting SafeHtml value is bound by the search-result template/product component, attacker-supplied HTML such as an event-handler payload can execute in the browser.

title: Search query reflected through bypassSecurityTrustHtml
description: The q query parameter is attacker-controlled and is explicitly converted into SafeHtml with bypassSecurityTrustHtml. The resulting searchValue is intended for HTML rendering, so a crafted URL can inject markup and script-capable event handlers into the search-results page. No sanitization or allowlist is applied before the security bypass.

trace.description: The component reads q from the current route's query parameters; the URL and its query string are controlled by the caller outside this file.
The query value is trimmed and also used as the table filter, but no HTML-specific validation or sanitization is performed before it is assigned to searchValue.

bypassSecurityTrustHtml marks the attacker-controlled query as trusted HTML. When searchValue is rendered by the component template, a crafted query containing HTML with an executable event handler can produce reflected client-side XSS.

title: Wallet address is submitted as authentication without signature proof
description: The component sends the connected wallet address to the backend without obtaining or verifying a cryptographic signature over a server-issued challenge. `provider.account` is only an identifier and is not proof that the caller controls the corresponding wallet. If `walletAddressSend` is used to establish wallet identity, authorize minting, or associate server-side actions with the wallet, an attacker can call the backend directly and substitute another user's address, potentially causing actions or state changes to be attributed to that victim wallet. The backend must issue a nonce and verify an EIP-191/EIP-712 signature, while binding the nonce to the session and chain.

trace.description: Angular invokes `ngOnInit` as a framework lifecycle entrypoint; the caller is outside this file and the component begins wallet authentication.
The component connects through the injected wallet and receives `provider.account`, but this operation produces only an address and no signed challenge or other proof of wallet control.
The address is copied directly into `metamaskAddress` and then used as the identity value sent to the application service.

`walletAddressSend` receives only the attacker- or client-supplied wallet address. No nonce, signature, signature verification result, or server-bound authentication token is supplied by this component before the backend processes the identity.

title: Plaintext credentials hardcoded in client-side source
description: The exported challenge instructions embed a real-looking email address and plaintext password directly in frontend source. These values are shipped to the browser and are explicitly exposed through the client-side code inspection workflow, allowing anyone who can load the application or inspect its bundle to obtain credentials and authenticate as the associated account. Even if intended for a testing challenge, hardcoded credentials in client-delivered code are exposed secrets and must not be used for any privileged or reusable account.

trace.description: The exported ExposedCredentialsInstruction object is consumed by a caller outside this file and defines the attacker-facing challenge workflow.
The workflow directs the user to inspect the client-side main.js bundle, making values embedded in these instructions or their compiled output discoverable to unauthenticated users.
The login email testing@juice-sh.op is hardcoded as the expected value for the frontend email field and is therefore exposed to anyone inspecting the client-side code.
The plaintext password IamUsedForTesting is hardcoded as the expected password and can be copied to log in as the associated account.

title: Plaintext Bender password hardcoded in frontend source
description: The frontend challenge instruction embeds Bender's plaintext password (`OhG0dPlease1nsertLiquor!`) in shipped client-side source as an argument to the password-input helper. Any user able to load or inspect the frontend bundle can recover the credential and use it to authenticate as Bender, resulting in account takeover if the credential remains valid. This is a hardcoded authentication secret exposed to clients.

trace.description: The exported challenge instruction is consumed by a caller outside this file and becomes part of the frontend application delivered to users.
The challenge workflow directs the user to enter an arbitrary password, while passing a literal password value to the helper as a special-case argument.

The plaintext credential `OhG0dPlease1nsertLiquor!` is embedded directly in source shipped to the browser. An attacker can inspect the JavaScript or source maps, recover it, and attempt direct authentication as Bender.

title: Jim's password hardcoded in frontend challenge code
description: The client-side challenge instruction embeds Jim's password as the literal `ncc-1701` in the password-field completion check. Because this TypeScript file is part of the frontend challenge bundle, an attacker who can inspect the shipped JavaScript or source maps can recover the credential and authenticate directly as Jim, bypassing the intended need to know the password. Although the challenge also teaches SQL injection, embedding a real account password in frontend code is independently exploitable credential exposure.

trace.description: The exported `LoginJimInstruction` challenge object is consumed by the frontend; its caller and bundling path are outside this file.

The challenge directs the user to enter an arbitrary nonempty password and passes the literal `ncc-1701` to the helper as the value that must not be entered, revealing that value in the client-side instruction logic.
The password literal `ncc-1701` is embedded directly in the frontend code. A user can inspect the bundle/source map, then submit this password to the normal login flow and authenticate as Jim.

title: Plaintext administrator credential embedded in frontend challenge code
description: The challenge instruction embeds the administrator's plaintext password, `admin123`, and guides a user through submitting it to the login form. If this frontend source or its compiled bundle is available to an attacker—as is typical for client-side code—the credential can be recovered and used to authenticate as the administrator, resulting in full administrative account compromise. Although this appears intentional for a hacking challenge, using a real privileged credential in shipped client-side code is an unsafe authentication and configuration practice.

trace.description: The exported `PasswordStrengthInstruction` object is consumed by a challenge runner outside this file; that external caller receives the instruction text and resolution callbacks.
The instruction explicitly identifies the administrator account and progressively reveals the password candidates, including the final value `admin123`, through client-side challenge logic.

The plaintext privileged password is supplied to the `#password` login field and the challenge then directs the user to click the login button, enabling authentication as the administrator by reusing the embedded credential.

title: Uninitialized challenge key causes accuracy calculation crash
description: The exported accuracy-calculation functions dereference `solves[challengeKey]` without first checking that the challenge key has been initialized. A caller outside this file can supply an unknown, stale, or otherwise invalid runtime value (TypeScript types do not enforce values at runtime), causing `solves[challengeKey][phase]` to throw a `TypeError`. If this exception is uncaught by the route or framework hook invoking the function, an attacker can repeatedly request accuracy for an uninitialized challenge and trigger application errors or denial of service.

trace.description: Caller outside this file supplies `challengeKey` to the exported `calculateFindItAccuracy` function; runtime input is not validated against an initialized entry in `solves`.
The exported function forwards the caller-controlled key to `calculateAccuracy` for the requested phase.
`calculateAccuracy` directly dereferences `solves[challengeKey][phase]`; for an unknown key, `solves[challengeKey]` is undefined and this access throws before returning an accuracy value.

title: Challenge flags broadcast to all connected Socket.IO clients
description: `sendNotification` builds a notification containing the challenge flag and broadcasts that object through Socket.IO. Because the function accepts a challenge object and does not restrict the recipient to the user who solved the challenge, every connected Socket.IO client can receive the flag whenever a challenge is solved or restored. An unauthorized client can therefore obtain challenge answers without completing the challenge, undermining challenge integrity and enabling unauthorized score/progress advancement.

trace.description: The exported `sendNotification` function receives a challenge object; its caller and any associated attacker-facing route are outside this file.
The function derives the challenge flag from the challenge name.
The derived flag is placed directly into the notification object that will be sent to clients.
The notification, including the flag, is emitted over the global Socket.IO instance without recipient or authorization filtering, exposing it to every connected client.

title: Unbounded FTP PDF cleanup can delay or exhaust service startup
description: The exported startup cleanup operation processes an unbounded number of matching files. A caller outside this file invokes `cleanupFtpFolder`, which uses `glob` to materialize every `ftp/*.pdf` path into memory and then performs an awaited removal for each file without a count limit, timeout, or other workload bound. If an attacker can place or cause large numbers of PDFs in the FTP directory, they can make startup cleanup consume significant memory and block the startup event loop for an attacker-controlled duration, potentially degrading availability or preventing the service from starting promptly.

trace.description: The exported `cleanupFtpFolder` function is the entrypoint; its caller and the mechanism allowing files into the FTP directory are outside this file.
The function calls `glob('ftp/*.pdf', ...)` and stores all matching paths in `files` without a maximum match count or resource bound.

The function awaits removal of every matched file sequentially. An attacker-controlled large file set therefore causes unbounded filesystem operations and startup delay, with no timeout or cancellation control.

title: Unescaped challenge keys enable regex injection and potential ReDoS
description: The challenge parser constructs regular expressions by interpolating the `challengeKey` directly into the pattern without escaping it. The key is extracted from scanned file contents, so a crafted or otherwise attacker-influenced source file can inject regex metacharacters and alter the matching expression. Combined with the greedy `.*` and `([^])*` portions, a malformed or adversarially large file can cause excessive backtracking during initialization, consuming CPU and potentially delaying or exhausting the process. Reachability depends on whether an attacker can influence files under the scanned paths.

trace.description: The exported `getCodeChallenges` function is the entrypoint; its caller is outside this file. It initializes the challenge parser and scans the configured source paths.
The function reads local files and extracts challenge keys directly from file contents. Those contents and derived keys are not constrained to a safe literal format before being passed to the parser.

`getCodeChallengesFromFile` derives `challengeKey` from source text and passes it to `getCodingChallengeFromFileContent`, where the key is interpolated into dynamically constructed regular expressions.

The `String.match` pattern embeds the unescaped `challengeKey` alongside greedy wildcard expressions. Regex metacharacters in the key can change the pattern, while large or malformed input can trigger excessive backtracking and CPU consumption.

title: noUpdate constraint can be bypassed for previously unset columns
description: The `noUpdate` constraint is bypassed whenever the protected column's previous value is `null` or `undefined`. The hook only raises a validation error when both checks at lines 36-37 pass, so a caller updating an initially unset immutable field can change it to an attacker-chosen value. Because the caller and update route are outside this file, the concrete impact depends on whether `column` protects an identity, ownership, authorization, or other integrity-sensitive field; the hook itself does not enforce immutability for unset values.

trace.description: The exported `makeKeyNonUpdatable` function is configured by a caller outside this file with a Sequelize model and the column intended to be immutable.
The function installs a `beforeValidate` hook that receives the model instance and examines its changed fields before validation.
For each changed field, the hook identifies the corresponding model attribute and checks whether it is the protected column.

The immutability error is raised only if the previous value is neither `undefined` nor `null`; when the protected field was previously unset, the condition is false and validation proceeds without rejecting the update.

title: noUpdate protection is bypassed when validation is disabled
description: The protection is conditionally disabled whenever Sequelize validation is invoked with `options.validate` false. The hook immediately returns before checking changed fields, allowing a caller outside this file to update the supposedly non-updatable column by using an update path that disables validation. This defeats the security/integrity guarantee represented by `makeKeyNonUpdatable`; the impact is unauthorized modification of whichever identity, ownership, or security-sensitive field is protected.

trace.description: The exported `makeKeyNonUpdatable` function is registered by a caller outside this file and is intended to enforce immutability for the supplied model column.
The installed validation hook receives update operations and their validation options from the external Sequelize caller.

The hook unconditionally returns when `options.validate` is false, without inspecting changed fields or the protected column, so an update performed with validation disabled reaches the update operation without the noUpdate check.

title: Unauthenticated WebSocket clients can delete global notifications
description: Any client that establishes a WebSocket connection can remove shared notification state without authentication or authorization. On connection, the server broadcasts every notification, including the value used as its deletion key, to the client. The client can then emit `notification received` with that flag; the handler finds the matching entry and splices it from the global `notifications` array. Because this state is shared across connections, an attacker can acknowledge or delete notifications before legitimate clients receive them, causing loss of challenge/security-event notifications and integrity-impacting denial of service.

trace.description: A WebSocket client connects to the Socket.IO server; the caller and any authentication context are outside this file, and no authentication or authorization check is performed in this connection handler.
For every connection, the server iterates over the shared global `notifications` collection.
Each notification is sent to the newly connected client, exposing the notification data, including the `flag` value later used as the deletion key.

The connected client can send the `notification received` event with attacker-controlled `data`; the handler accepts it without checking the sender's identity or whether the notification was assigned to that client.
The attacker-controlled value is compared directly against notification flags to select a shared notification entry.
When a match is found, the handler removes it from the shared global collection, allowing one unauthenticated client to suppress notifications for other clients.

title: Dependency-checker exceptions cause an uncaught startup failure
description: If the dependency checker throws for an invalid, inaccessible, or otherwise problematic package directory, the catch block logs the error but leaves `dependencies` as its initial empty object. Execution then enters the failure branch and iterates `dependencies.error`, which is undefined, causing a new uncaught `TypeError`. A caller that supplies or derives `packageDir` externally can therefore turn dependency validation into an exception and potentially prevent application startup or disrupt the startup process instead of receiving the intended validation failure result.

trace.description: The exported function receives `packageDir` from a caller outside this file; the value determines which package directory is checked.

The externally supplied directory is passed to `dependencyChecker`. If dependency checking fails, the exception is caught and only logged; `dependencies` remains the empty object initialized before the try block.
The failure branch unconditionally iterates `dependencies.error`, but that property is absent after a caught exception, producing an uncaught `TypeError` and interrupting the validation/startup flow.

title: Mass assignment allows clients to control Address.UserId ownership
description: The Address model exposes the ownership field `UserId` as a normal writable attribute, with no model-level allowlist or protection preventing the generated CRUD handlers from binding caller-supplied properties. The auto-generated `POST /api/Addresss` and `PUT /api/Addresss/:id` routes are outside this file, but they consume this model and can therefore persist a request body's `UserId` value. An attacker can create or modify an address with another user's ID, reassigning ownership and potentially causing the address to appear in that user's address set or enabling subsequent unauthorized use of the address. The same implicit-binding design also makes future sensitive model fields writable by default.

trace.description: Attacker-facing generated CRUD entrypoints `POST /api/Addresss` and `PUT /api/Addresss/:id` are outside this file; their request bodies are bound to the exported Address model.
The Address schema declares `UserId` as a regular model attribute without marking it server-managed, immutable, or otherwise restricting caller assignment.

`UserId` is initialized as a persisted column in the `Addresses` table, so an implicitly bound request property can be stored as the address owner. No explicit field allowlist is present in the model initialization.

title: XML parser enables filesystem-backed external entity resolution (XXE)
description: The exported parser accepts attacker-controlled XML and deliberately enables both entity substitution (XML_PARSE_NOENT) and DTD loading (XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD). It also registers filesystem input providers, allowing external entities such as file:///etc/passwd to be resolved. An attacker who can supply XML containing a SYSTEM external entity can cause local file contents to be read and incorporated into the returned XML string, resulting in sensitive-file disclosure. This configuration also permits entity-expansion denial of service, with the timeout not constituting a reliable restriction on native parser and filesystem activity.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported parseXmlString function receives the attacker-controlled XML string through its data parameter.
The parser host registers filesystem input providers, explicitly enabling resolution of external entities such as file:///etc/passwd.
The XML parsing options enable DTD loading and entity substitution, so external entity declarations in the supplied XML are resolved rather than treated as inert data.
The attacker-controlled XML is passed to libxml2's XML parser with those unsafe options, causing external entities to be fetched and their contents embedded in the parsed document.
