title: Unrestricted server-side fetch of configured asset URLs
description: Custom file configuration is treated as an arbitrary download URL. If an attacker can influence the application configuration (for example through a deployment/configuration management interface), they can set an application asset such as `application.logo`, `application.favicon`, or `application.promotion.video` to an internal HTTP(S) endpoint. `utils.isUrl` only identifies URLs and no host, scheme, or resolved-IP allowlist is applied before the server fetches the resource. This can expose cloud metadata, internal administrative services, or other network-reachable resources to the attacker through the downloaded asset or resulting application behavior.

The attacker-influenced URL is passed to `utils.downloadToFile`, causing the server to make an outbound request to an arbitrary destination such as `http://127.0.0.1/` or a cloud metadata endpoint.

title: Unescaped configuration values injected into frontend HTML
description: Application customization values are concatenated directly into HTML replacement text and written into the served `index.html`. In particular, cookie-consent fields such as the message, link text, and link URL are not HTML- or JavaScript-escaped. An attacker who can influence the configuration can inject markup or script-bearing content (for example, by breaking out of an attribute/string context), which will be served to frontend users and can enable stored client-side code execution or malicious links.

The constructed attacker-influenced text is supplied as the replacement to a file rewrite operation targeting the served frontend `index.html`; the browser subsequently interprets the injected markup in that document.

title: Unvalidated webhook URL enables server-side request forgery and data exfiltration

If an attacker can influence this argument through a caller outside this file, they can cause the server to issue a POST to loopback, cloud metadata services, private network hosts, or attacker-controlled infrastructure. The request body discloses challenge solution data, the CTF flag, hostname, OS details, application name, environment, and version to the selected destination.

description: `downloadToFile` downloads the complete remote response into memory via `download(url)` and only then writes it to disk. There is no response-size limit, timeout, or streaming/backpressure control in this wrapper. An attacker who can supply the URL can point it at a very large or slow resource, consuming server memory and connections and potentially causing denial of service.

title: Mass assignment allows caller-controlled Feedback UserId

Because UserId is accepted as a normal model property and is not derived from the authenticated session in this file, an attacker can submit another user's ID and create feedback attributed to that user, corrupting ownership and attribution data. The route implementation is outside this file, so confidence is based on the documented auto-generated CRUD behavior.

Because the ownership value is taken from the request rather than being derived from the authenticated session, this can create cross-user records and undermine later ownership checks.

An attacker can therefore submit an authenticated upgrade request with an unsupported or absent payment mode and have their role changed to deluxe without charge.

After the payment branches, the handler unconditionally updates the selected customer's role to `deluxe` and issues a deluxe token, granting the paid privilege without successful payment.

title: Concurrent deluxe upgrades can overdraw wallet balances
description: The wallet payment flow is vulnerable to a check-then-use race. Two concurrent authenticated upgrade requests can both read a wallet balance of at least 49 at line 26, pass the check, and then each execute the unconditional decrement at line 30. The decrement has no balance predicate and is not enclosed with the balance check and membership update in a transaction, so concurrent requests can overdraw the wallet while still completing the deluxe upgrade.

`WalletModel.decrement` unconditionally subtracts 49 for the user after the prior non-atomic check, allowing multiple concurrent requests to drive the wallet below its available balance.

title: CAPTCHA solution disclosed to unauthenticated clients
description: The unauthenticated CAPTCHA endpoint returns both the challenge and its solution in the JSON response. An attacker can request a CAPTCHA, read the `answer` field, and submit that value with any protected-by-CAPTCHA request such as POST /api/Feedbacks, defeating the anti-automation control.

The handler generates the CAPTCHA expression and computes its answer, then places both values into the response object.
The generated CAPTCHA record, including the answer, is persisted, but no confidentiality or server-side-only handling is applied to the solution.
The response serializes and returns `captcha`, including `answer`, to the unauthenticated requester. The requester can therefore trivially satisfy verifyCaptcha without solving the challenge.

title: CAPTCHA challenges are reusable after successful verification
description: CAPTCHA verification checks whether a matching record and answer exist, but does not invalidate or delete the record after successful verification. A client can reuse the same captchaId and answer for repeated requests, bypassing the intended single-use nature of a CAPTCHA challenge. Because the solution is also returned by GET /rest/captcha, the attacker can obtain a valid reusable pair directly.

The middleware looks up a CAPTCHA solely by the supplied captchaId.
It accepts the request when the supplied answer matches, without checking expiration, binding the challenge to a client, or marking the record as consumed.
Successful verification calls `next()` and leaves the CAPTCHA record available for future identical submissions, enabling replay of the same CAPTCHA pair.

title: Unauthenticated CAPTCHA generation permits unbounded database growth
description: The unauthenticated CAPTCHA-generation endpoint performs a database insert on every request and has no visible rate limit, quota, cleanup, or other resource bound. An attacker can repeatedly call GET /rest/captcha to create unbounded CAPTCHA rows and consume database/storage resources, potentially degrading availability.

Each invocation allocates a new CAPTCHA identifier and generates a new challenge.
Each request builds a new persistent CaptchaModel instance; no per-client or global request limit is enforced in this handler.
The handler saves one database record for every request, allowing repeated requests to grow persistent storage without bound.

title: ZIP path traversal allows unauthenticated arbitrary file overwrite
description: The unauthenticated POST /file-upload route accepts a ZIP file and passes its entries to extractZipBuffer when the file-write challenge is enabled. The path-traversal check tests whether the resolved path merely contains the current working directory string, rather than verifying that it is inside the intended uploads/complaints directory. An archive entry such as ../../.env or ../../routes/fileUpload.ts resolves within the application working directory, passes the check, and is then written using the traversal-containing path. An attacker can therefore overwrite arbitrary files reachable under the application working directory, including configuration or application files, causing data integrity loss and potentially code execution on restart.

For a .zip filename, the handler sends the attacker-controlled buffer to extractZipBuffer when the file-write challenge is enabled.

The containment check is insufficient: absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.')) accepts paths that escape uploads/complaints but remain anywhere under the process working directory, such as ../../.env or ../../routes/fileUpload.ts.
The ZIP entry is written using the original relative entry path, allowing the traversal path to overwrite the resolved target file.

title: Unauthenticated file upload has no effective size or expansion limits
description: The upload-size middleware is effectively a no-op: checkUploadSize performs no size check and always calls next(). The /file-upload route uses in-memory multipart storage before this middleware, and ZIP processing then buffers and parses the complete upload and processes every archive entry. An attacker can submit very large files, archives with many entries, or highly expanding compressed content to consume process memory, CPU, and disk space. The unauthenticated route makes this remotely triggerable and can degrade or exhaust service resources.

The registered checkUploadSize middleware does not inspect the file size or reject anything; it unconditionally advances the request.
ZIP handling loads the complete upload buffer into an archive directory and iterates over all entries, with no compressed-size, expanded-size, entry-count, or processing limit.

title: Windows path traversal in key-file serving route
description: The handler accepts an attacker-controlled route parameter and attempts to prevent traversal only by rejecting forward slashes. Because it uses the platform-native `path.resolve`, a Windows deployment will treat backslashes as path separators. A request such as `GET /.../..%5c..%5cWindows%5cwin.ini` can therefore pass the check and cause `sendFile` to read a file outside the `encryptionkeys` directory. This results in arbitrary local file disclosure on Windows deployments, subject to the process account's filesystem permissions.

The route parameter is copied directly into `file` without canonicalization or an allow-list of permitted key filenames.

`path.resolve` canonicalizes the attacker-controlled path and `res.sendFile` serves the resulting file, allowing a Windows backslash traversal to escape `encryptionkeys/`.

title: Data export accepts an unverified user identifier for memory retrieval
description: The authenticated data-export handler uses the caller-controlled `req.body.UserId` to retrieve memories, but never verifies that this identifier equals the authenticated user's ID. The route has authentication middleware, but authentication alone does not establish ownership of the requested user record; the handler's authorization decision relies on the middleware having overwritten or safely constrained this body field. If `UserId` remains attacker-controlled or the handler is reused without that middleware, User A can submit User B's ID and receive User B's memory captions and image paths in the export. This is a BOLA/access-control flaw in the handler's data flow.

The retrieved memories are copied into the export response, including each memory's image URL and caption, allowing an attacker who controls the identifier to receive another user's memory data.

title: Attacker-controlled layout enables arbitrary local file disclosure and template interpretation
description: The POST handler accepts a caller-controlled `layout` value and passes it into the rendering context without an allow-list or confinement to the application's template directory. Although the code resolves the path and blocks a few filename substrings, it does not restrict the path to an approved directory, so alternate local paths can bypass the blacklist. With the application's layout-aware rendering configuration, an attacker can cause arbitrary local files to be loaded and rendered, exposing their contents; files containing template directives may also be interpreted by the template engine.

The original request body, including the attacker-controlled `layout`, is spread into the render locals. The fixed `dataErasureResult` view is then rendered with that value, allowing the configured layout renderer to resolve and process the selected local template/file.

title: Windows path traversal in log file serving
description: The exported handler accepts the attacker-controlled `params.file` value and passes it to `path.resolve('logs/', file)` after checking only for forward slashes. On Windows, backslashes are path separators, so a value such as `..\..\config\secrets.json` or `C:\Windows\win.ini` contains no forward slash, bypasses the check, and causes `res.sendFile` to read a file outside the intended `logs/` directory. An attacker who can reach the route can therefore disclose arbitrary readable files, including application configuration or secrets. Exploitability is platform-dependent; the check is insufficient on Windows.

The only validation rejects `/`. On Windows, attacker-supplied backslashes or an absolute drive-letter path bypass this check, and `path.resolve` can resolve outside the `logs/` directory before `res.sendFile` serves the resulting file.

title: Sensitive KeePass database exposed through public file server
description: The public file-serving handler explicitly allowlists `incident-support.kdbx`, causing a sensitive KeePass database to be served through the same unauthenticated file-download path as public documentation. An attacker who supplies that filename can retrieve the credential vault, potentially enabling offline password cracking and disclosure of stored secrets.

title: Windows path traversal bypasses file-server directory restriction

title: Race condition permits duplicate likes and review data corruption
description: The like operation is vulnerable to a race condition that allows duplicate likes and corrupts the relationship between `likesCount` and `likedBy`. Two concurrent requests from the same authenticated user can both pass the membership check before either request records the user. Each request then increments `likesCount` independently at line 35 and later appends the same email and overwrites `likedBy` at line 49. Depending on timing, the result can contain duplicate user entries or a count that exceeds the number of recorded users. The 150 ms artificial delay widens the race window. An attacker can send concurrent requests for the same review ID to inflate likes or corrupt review data.

The handler increments `likesCount` in a separate database update before recording the user's email. Concurrent requests can each increment the count.
The deliberate 150 ms delay increases the interval during which concurrent requests can pass the check and operate on stale state.

The handler appends the user's email to the fetched array and writes the entire `likedBy` array back with `$set`, without an atomic uniqueness constraint or conditional update. Concurrent requests can write duplicate emails or overwrite one another, leaving `likesCount` inconsistent with `likedBy`.

title: SQL injection in login enables authentication bypass
description: The unauthenticated login handler interpolates the caller-controlled `req.body.email` directly into a raw SQL query. An attacker can submit an email such as `' OR 1=1 --` so the query condition is altered and the password predicate is commented out, potentially causing an arbitrary user row to be returned and allowing authentication without the user's password. The query uses Sequelize's raw `sequelize.query` but provides no bound parameters or allow-listing.

title: Login endpoint lacks brute-force rate limiting
description: The public login endpoint performs an unrestricted database authentication query for every request and contains no per-IP, per-account, or per-endpoint throttling, lockout, or backoff. An attacker can issue large numbers of login attempts, consuming database/application resources and enabling high-volume password brute force. Network-level controls may mitigate this, but no application-level control is present in this file.

Each request proceeds directly to authentication processing; `verifyPreLoginChallenges` is empty and does not provide a throttle or lockout control.

title: Unbounded retrieval and in-memory reversal of all orders

The handler accepts no pagination, limit, or other bound, so a caller with accounting access can repeatedly trigger retrieval and in-memory materialization of every order as the collection grows, consuming database resources and application memory and potentially degrading or exhausting service capacity.

title: NFT challenge can be claimed using another user's wallet address
description: The unauthenticated wallet verification endpoint accepts a caller-supplied `walletAddress` and treats its presence in the process-wide `addressesMinted` set as proof that the caller owns that wallet or performed the mint. The handler performs no wallet signature verification, authenticated-session binding, or on-chain ownership check. Because wallet addresses and NFT mint events are publicly discoverable, an attacker can submit another user's recently minted address and receive the successful challenge status before the legitimate user does. The address is then deleted, making this a claim-stealing authorization bypass.

The handler receives the caller-controlled request body and copies `req.body.walletAddress` into `metamaskAddress` without requiring a signed message or binding it to the authenticated user.
The caller-supplied address is used as the sole identity/proof check against the global set of addresses observed in NFT mint events; there is no ownership or authorization check.
If the address is present, the handler deletes it and returns `success: true` with the challenge status, allowing the attacker to solve the challenge using another user's mint.

title: Unbounded public memory listing enables resource-exhaustion attacks
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/memories endpoint performs an unbounded query for every memory and eagerly includes the associated UserModel. There is no pagination, limit, result cap, or other application-level control. An attacker can repeatedly request this public endpoint as the number of stored memories grows, forcing the application and database to load and serialize the complete collection, potentially causing excessive memory/CPU usage and service degradation.

title: CAPTCHA answer disclosed in API response

An authenticated caller can read `answer` directly and submit it to any endpoint protected by `verifyImageCaptcha`, defeating the CAPTCHA control without solving the image. The response also exposes the associated internal `UserId` value.

The complete object, including the plaintext CAPTCHA answer, is returned to the requester as JSON. The requester can copy this value into `req.body.answer` and bypass the intended CAPTCHA challenge.

Therefore a caller can skip the CAPTCHA-generation step and invoke the protected workflow directly. The registered POST route applies `security.appendUserId()` but no authentication middleware is listed, further increasing the risk that downstream processing relies on this middleware as a gate.

The middleware derives the user ID from the request and searches for a recent CAPTCHA belonging to that ID. If no authenticated user is present, the lookup uses an undefined `UserId` rather than rejecting the request.
The query is limited to recent CAPTCHA records, but an empty result is not treated as a verification failure.

The condition explicitly calls `next()` whenever `captchas[0]` is missing, without checking `req.body.answer`. An attacker can omit CAPTCHA creation or use an account with no recent CAPTCHA and proceed to the downstream data-export handler.

title: Unauthenticated access to premium content bypasses payment gate
description: The premium-content route is publicly reachable without authentication or any payment/entitlement check. The handler directly serves the protected wallpaper, so an unauthenticated attacker can request the route and obtain content that the application claims is behind a BTC payment gate, bypassing the intended access-control and payment workflow.

The handler unconditionally sends the premium wallpaper file to the requester, without verifying payment, entitlement, authentication, or any other authorization condition.

title: Unauthenticated checkout of arbitrary baskets

The handler checks only whether the basket exists; it never verifies that the requester owns it or is authorized to check it out. An unauthenticated attacker can submit another user's basket ID, consume its items, clear its coupon and create an order for it. This is a broken object-level authorization vulnerability.

The target basket identifier is taken directly from the request path.

The only check after lookup is whether a basket exists, not whether it belongs to the authenticated requester. The authenticated user's email is read later but is not used for authorization.
The handler destroys all basket items for the supplied basket ID and returns an order confirmation, allowing an unauthenticated caller to complete and mutate another user's basket.

title: Client-controlled UserId enables unauthorized wallet mutations

It does not derive the user ID from the authenticated session or verify that the supplied ID belongs to the requester. An unauthenticated attacker can submit a victim's UserId with paymentId='wallet' and cause the victim's wallet to be debited for the attacker-selected basket, or cause bonus points to be credited to an arbitrary account. This is an authorization failure over a sensitive account resource and a client-controlled payment workflow.

The selected account's balance is decremented, so supplying another user's ID can charge that user's wallet for the checkout.
The same caller-selected account is also credited with order bonus points, allowing arbitrary account mutation through a client-supplied identity field.

title: Unauthenticated access to recycle items by ID
description: The recycle-item endpoint is reachable without authentication or authorization and uses the caller-supplied path identifier directly to retrieve a record. An attacker can request another user's recycle item by substituting its numeric ID and receive the serialized record, because there is no per-record ownership or role check before the response is sent. This enables unauthenticated object-level data access (and BOLA if recycle records are user-owned).

The result of RecycleModel.findAll (line 12) is serialized and sent to the requester without any authorization or ownership verification. A caller can substitute another record's ID and obtain that recycle item's data.

title: Windows path traversal in quarantine file serving

This bypasses the intended directory boundary and can expose sensitive host files when the application runs on Windows.

title: Client-controlled login IP is persisted as trusted account data

There is no trusted-proxy validation or comparison against the socket address. Consequently, any authenticated caller can submit an arbitrary value and poison the account's recorded login IP. If this field is used for IP-based security decisions, auditing, anomaly detection, or account-recovery controls elsewhere, those controls can be bypassed or rendered unreliable. The route is externally reachable without route middleware, although the handler does perform an application-level authenticated-user check.

The handler obtains the current authenticated user, but the request remains able to control the `true-client-ip` header independently of that identity.

The `true-client-ip` header is read directly from the request and, after only sanitization intended for content safety, is treated as the login IP. No trusted-proxy validation or server-side source verification is performed.
The attacker-controlled value is persisted to the authenticated user's `lastLoginIp` field, poisoning security-relevant account metadata.

title: Unauthenticated password reset is vulnerable to online security-answer brute force
description: The unauthenticated password-reset endpoint performs an account password mutation after validating only an email address and security-question answer, but the declared route has no authentication or rate-limiting middleware. An attacker can repeatedly submit guesses for low-entropy security answers, causing repeated database lookups and HMAC computations until the answer is accepted, then set a new password for the targeted account. This enables account takeover and also permits abusive load against the reset operation.

After a successful answer guess, the handler directly updates the located user's password with the attacker-supplied value, completing account takeover; repeated requests also repeatedly consume database and HMAC resources.

title: Unauthenticated and forgeable continue codes allow arbitrary challenge completion

The Hashids salts are hardcoded in the source, so the continue codes are forgeable rather than functioning as unforgeable authorization tokens: an attacker can encode arbitrary challenge IDs and mark challenges as solved, bypassing intended challenge/workflow requirements and potentially affecting other users if state is shared.

title: SQL injection in product search query

An attacker can submit SQL metacharacters such as `q=' OR 1=1 --` to alter the WHERE clause, potentially bypassing the intended product filtering and exposing records that should not match the search. The 200-character truncation limits length but does not provide SQL parameterization or safe structural validation.

A caller can repeatedly issue broad searches such as an empty query or `%` to force full-table scans, sorting, and unbounded response materialization, potentially degrading availability as the product table grows.

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of arbitrary users' security questions

There is no authentication or per-user authorization check tying the requested email to the caller. An attacker can submit another user's email to enumerate whether an account exists and obtain the security question used in the account-recovery/authentication workflow, assisting targeted security-answer guessing and account takeover attempts.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported handler registered for GET /rest/user/security-question without authentication. The handler receives the attacker-controlled query object.

The handler reads the caller-supplied email query parameter and uses it to locate a SecurityAnswer joined to a User. No authentication or ownership/authorization check is performed before this lookup.
The email value is used as the User lookup criterion, allowing an attacker to substitute any target user's email address.

After finding the matching answer record, the handler loads the referenced security question and returns it to the unauthenticated caller. Supplying another user's email therefore discloses that user's recovery question.

title: NoSQL JavaScript injection through the product ID in MongoDB $where
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/products/:id/reviews handler receives the product identifier from the request and, when the NoSQL command challenge is enabled, only truncates the value before concatenating it into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. Truncation is not an allow-list or parameterization control, so an attacker can supply JavaScript syntax in :id and have it evaluated by MongoDB. This can alter the query predicate, expose reviews for unintended products, or trigger expensive/arbitrary server-side JavaScript behavior, including denial of service and potentially database-side code execution depending on MongoDB server-side JavaScript configuration.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported middleware for the unauthenticated GET /rest/products/:id/reviews route; the attacker controls req.params.id.

The route uses the attacker-controlled path parameter directly when the NoSQL command challenge is enabled. utils.trunc(req.params.id, 40) only limits length and does not restrict JavaScript syntax or make the value a data parameter.

The truncated value is concatenated into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression and executed by the database. No parameterization or effective allow-list intervenes, allowing injected expression syntax to change query behavior or cause expensive/server-side JavaScript execution.

title: Unauthenticated triggering of solved-challenge notifications
description: The unauthenticated `GET /rest/repeat-notification` handler accepts an arbitrary challenge name and triggers `sendNotification` whenever the globally found challenge is marked solved. It performs no authentication, user association, or authorization check tying the challenge to the caller. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore repeatedly invoke notifications for any solved challenge, causing unauthorized notification activity and potentially affecting other connected clients if notifications are broadcast.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller is outside this file; the exported handler is registered as unauthenticated `GET /rest/repeat-notification`, so any remote caller can reach the returned request handler.

The attacker controls the `challenge` query parameter, which is URL-decoded and used to select a challenge by name. The only condition checked later is whether the challenge is solved; there is no check that the caller is authenticated or is the user who solved it.
The attacker-controlled challenge name selects the challenge record through `findChallengeByName` without any per-user ownership or authorization constraint.
For any selected solved challenge, the handler invokes `sendNotification` without authorization, allowing an unauthenticated caller to trigger the notification side effect repeatedly.

title: Authenticated users can modify arbitrary product reviews
description: The authenticated PATCH /rest/products/reviews handler accepts a review identifier from req.body.id and updates the matching review without checking that the authenticated user owns or authored it. The authenticated user is retrieved at line 15 but never used for an ownership or authorization constraint. Any logged-in user can substitute another user's review ID and change its message, causing unauthorized cross-user modification and data integrity loss.

trace.description: The caller outside this file invokes the exported handler for PATCH /rest/products/reviews; the route is protected only by authentication middleware.
The handler obtains the authenticated user, but does not use that identity to constrain the target review or verify ownership.
The attacker-controlled request body field req.body.id selects the review to modify, while req.body.message supplies the replacement content.
The database update matches by _id alone and uses multi: true, with no author/user ownership predicate, then persists the supplied message.

title: NoSQL operator injection enables mass review tampering
description: The request body controls the value used as the MongoDB _id query criterion without enforcing that it is a scalar identifier. An attacker can submit an operator object such as {"$ne": null} (subject to the application's MongoDB driver behavior), turning the selector into a broad query. Because the update uses multi: true, this can modify every matching review by setting their message to attacker-controlled content. This is NoSQL operator injection with a mass data-integrity impact.

trace.description: The caller outside this file invokes the exported PATCH /rest/products/reviews handler with attacker-controlled JSON request data.
The request body is accepted without validating that id is a scalar review identifier rather than an object containing MongoDB query operators.
The untrusted id value is embedded directly as the _id selector in a MongoDB update query; an operator object can alter the query semantics, and multi: true permits updating all matching documents.

title: Unauthenticated access to arbitrary orders via order ID
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/track-order/:id handler accepts a caller-controlled order identifier and queries the orders collection without checking authentication, ownership, or authorization. An attacker can substitute another customer's order ID and receive that order's data in the JSON response. The caller/route registration is outside this file, but the exported handler receives the attacker-controlled request.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives an attacker-controlled Express request for GET /rest/track-order/:id, and the route is registered without authentication middleware.
The target resource identifier is taken directly from req.params.id and assigned to id.
The handler looks up orders using only the supplied orderId. There is no authentication, ownership predicate, or per-order authorization check before the result is returned.
The matching order data is serialized and sent to the caller with res.json(result). User A can replace the path ID with User B's order ID and obtain User B's order information.

title: MongoDB $where JavaScript injection through order ID
description: When reflectedXssChallenge is enabled, the handler only truncates req.params.id and does not sanitize or parameterize it before embedding it into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. A payload such as `' || true || '` can alter the generated expression from an equality check into a condition that evaluates true, causing arbitrary orders to match and potentially enabling JavaScript-expression injection in the database query context. The non-challenge branch strips characters, but the weaker challenge-enabled branch is reachable by design when that challenge is enabled.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives the attacker-controlled :id path parameter for GET /rest/track-order/:id.
When reflectedXssChallenge is enabled, req.params.id is merely truncated to 60 characters, leaving quote and JavaScript syntax characters intact.

The untrusted id is interpolated directly into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. For example, an input containing `' || true || '` changes the expression structure instead of remaining a data value; no parameterization or effective allow-list is applied in this branch.
MongoDB evaluates the constructed $where expression as query code, allowing the attacker to change query semantics and retrieve unintended orders.

title: Unauthenticated unbounded in-memory profile image upload enables denial of service
description: The POST /profile/image/file route uses an in-memory upload middleware before this handler performs authentication. The handler accepts the already-buffered `req.file`/`req.file.buffer` without any visible size limit, and then passes the entire attacker-controlled buffer to `fileType.fromBuffer`. Because authentication is checked only afterward, an unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly submit oversized multipart files, causing memory allocation and file-type processing before being rejected. This can exhaust application memory and degrade or crash the service. The route's upstream `uploadToMemory.single('file')` middleware is outside this file, so its configuration cannot be verified here; no compensating size limit is present in this handler.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file registers `profileImageFileUpload()` for `POST /profile/image/file` with `uploadToMemory.single('file')` before the handler and without authentication middleware.

The handler receives `req.file` and its complete in-memory buffer. This data has already been materialized by the upstream memory-storage upload middleware before the handler reaches its authentication check.

The entire attacker-controlled buffer is passed to `fileType.fromBuffer` with no size check or bounded processing. Authentication is not checked until later at lines 35-39, so unauthenticated requests can force memory and CPU consumption before rejection.

The unbounded buffer is subsequently written to disk after authentication, with no per-request size or upload quota enforced in this handler; repeated large authenticated uploads can also consume disk and I/O resources.

title: Unbounded in-memory growth from unauthenticated feedback requests
description: The public POST /api/Feedbacks route invokes captchaBypassChallenge without authentication or any rate-limiting control. Each request writes a timestamp into req.app.locals.captchaBypassReqTimes at a monotonically increasing index and increments the global captchaReqId. Because neither value is bounded or periodically reclaimed in this file, an attacker can repeatedly submit requests to grow the in-memory array indefinitely, causing increasing memory consumption and potentially process exhaustion or denial of service.

trace.description: Attacker-controlled requests reach the exported captchaBypassChallenge middleware through the caller outside this file; the middleware is registered on the unauthenticated POST /api/Feedbacks route.
For every request, the middleware uses the global captchaReqId as a new array index and records the current timestamp, with no maximum size, eviction, or rate limit.
The global request counter is incremented after each write, ensuring subsequent requests continue allocating new array entries rather than reusing bounded storage.
The unbounded array assignment is the resource-consumption sink: repeated unauthenticated requests can exhaust application memory and degrade or terminate the process.

title: Authenticated server-side request forgery via profile image URL
description: The handler accepts an attacker-controlled `req.body.imageUrl` and passes it directly to `fetch()` without an allowlist, scheme restriction, private-network blocking, redirect validation, or resolved-IP validation. Any authenticated user can therefore cause the server to make requests to internal services such as localhost administration endpoints, cloud metadata services, or private network hosts. The response body is then consumed by the application, enabling SSRF-based access to otherwise unreachable resources.

trace.description: The exported middleware is invoked for `POST /profile/image/url`; its caller and route registration are outside this file. The handler receives attacker-controlled request data through `req`.
The handler reads `req.body.imageUrl` and only checks that it is defined. The value is not restricted to approved domains, protocols, or non-private destinations.
The user-controlled URL is passed directly to `fetch()` after only checking that the user has a token recognized by the in-memory authentication map.

title: Unbounded remote response download enables denial of service
description: The URL-fetching endpoint streams the entire response from an attacker-controlled server into an on-disk file without enforcing a response-size limit, checking Content-Length, applying a timeout, or otherwise bounding transfer duration. An authenticated attacker can point `imageUrl` at a server that returns an arbitrarily large or indefinitely slow response, consuming disk space, file descriptors, memory, and request resources and potentially causing denial of service.

trace.description: The exported middleware handles attacker-controlled input for `POST /profile/image/url`; the route caller is outside this file.
`req.body.imageUrl` is accepted as the remote source URL after only an authentication check; no download size or time limit is configured here.

The complete response body is converted to a stream and piped into a file, with no byte cap, timeout, or cancellation mechanism. A malicious remote server can therefore cause an arbitrarily large or indefinitely running download.

title: Arbitrary wallet credit creation during balance top-up
description: The wallet top-up endpoint accepts the caller-controlled `req.body.balance` amount and directly increments the authenticated user's wallet after checking only that a card record exists. There is no server-side validation of the amount, charge authorization, payment processing, or correlation between the amount and an actual transaction. An authenticated user with any registered card can submit an arbitrarily large positive balance and create wallet credit without paying the corresponding amount, causing financial/data-integrity loss.

trace.description: PUT /rest/wallet/balance invokes the exported `addWalletBalance` handler; the route caller and request authentication context are outside this file.

The handler reads the caller-supplied `paymentId` and `balance` fields. It verifies only that the referenced card belongs to `req.body.UserId`; it does not validate the requested amount or establish that a payment for that amount was completed.

The unbounded caller-supplied `req.body.balance` is passed to `WalletModel.increment`, directly creating wallet credit. Supplying a very large positive amount with any valid owned card increases the wallet without a corresponding payment.

title: Prototype-key denial of service in code-fix cache lookup
description: Both unauthenticated routes pass attacker-controlled keys into `readFixes()`. The cache is a plain object, and the lookup at line 21 does not restrict access to own properties. Supplying a key such as `__proto__` or `constructor` returns an inherited Object prototype member/function instead of a `codeFix`. The handlers then dereference `fixData.fixes.length`, which is absent, causing a TypeError and an error response for each request. Repeated requests can generate application errors and consume server resources, providing a low-impact denial-of-service condition.

The attacker-controlled key is passed directly to `readFixes(key)`; the POST handler does the same with `req.body.key`.
`CodeFixes` is a normal object and the lookup does not use an own-property check. Keys such as `__proto__` and `constructor` resolve inherited properties rather than a `codeFix` record.

The handler assumes the result is a valid `codeFix` and accesses `.fixes.length`; inherited prototype values do not provide this property, causing a TypeError and repeated error handling/resource consumption.

title: Information disclosure in /rest error response
description: The externally reachable GET /rest/unrecognized path returns a 500 error page containing the configured application name and the attacker-supplied unexpected path. An unauthenticated attacker can use malformed or probing requests to fingerprint the application and obtain reflected request details in error responses, aiding reconnaissance and potentially exposing internal error-handling behavior.

The test sends an unauthenticated GET request to /rest/unrecognized and confirms that the application responds with HTTP 500.
The response body is consumed as an HTML error page containing the configured application name and the unexpected request path, demonstrating information leakage to the requester.

title: Unbounded attacker-controlled growth of global wallet set
description: The unauthenticated wallet-exploit endpoint accepts an arbitrary `walletAddress` value and inserts it into the process-global `walletsConnected` Set without validation, expiration, size bound, or rate limiting. An attacker can submit a large number of distinct values, causing the Set to grow indefinitely for the lifetime of the process and consume memory, potentially degrading or terminating the service. The caller and route registration are outside this file, but the exported handler is directly reachable from that route without authentication.

Each request adds the attacker-controlled value to the process-global Set. Distinct values remain retained indefinitely because entries are removed only when a matching blockchain exploitation event occurs; there is no cap, expiration, rate limit, or cleanup for unrecognized values.

title: Hardcoded Ethereum private key committed to test source
description: The test source hardcodes an Ethereum private key and submits it to the Web3 endpoint. Anyone with access to the repository, published source package, or generated test artifacts can reuse this credential to derive the corresponding wallet identity and potentially control any assets held by that wallet. Private keys should be injected through protected test configuration or generated ephemerally rather than committed to source.

The test places the hardcoded private key into the request body for the Web3 key-submission workflow.
The private key is transmitted to `/rest/web3/submitKey`, demonstrating that the committed credential is actively used as an authentication/unlock credential rather than merely being inert test data.

title: Hardcoded and weak account credentials in test source
description: The test source contains hardcoded account credentials, including the administrator password `admin123` and passwords for other customer, accountant, and CISO accounts. Anyone who gains access to the repository or deployed test artifacts can extract these credentials and authenticate as those users; the administrator credential is especially weak and may be reused in a reachable environment. These are embedded directly in source rather than supplied through a protected test-secret mechanism.

The test constructs authentication requests by passing literal account email addresses and passwords to the shared login helper.
A privileged administrator password is hardcoded as `admin123` in the source and is used for authentication. Repository or artifact disclosure therefore exposes a directly usable, weak credential.

title: Orphaned basket items can be reassigned to an arbitrary basket
description: An authenticated caller can create a basket item without a BasketId and then update that orphaned item to assign an arbitrary BasketId. The test expects this reassignment to return 200 and confirms BasketId 3 in the response. BasketId is the resource-ownership boundary for basket items; allowing it to be set after creation without an ownership check can let a user attach items to another user's basket and modify their cart. The normal update path rejects changing an already-set BasketId, but the missing-initial-value case bypasses that control.

The caller first creates a basket item without supplying BasketId, and the test expects creation to succeed with BasketId undefined, producing an orphaned item.
The caller then supplies BasketId 3 in the update request, using the previously orphaned item as a vehicle to change its basket association.

The test asserts that the server accepts the reassignment with HTTP 200 and returns BasketId 3, demonstrating that the ownership-related association can be changed after creation without an evidenced per-basket authorization check.

title: Plaintext account passwords committed in delivery API tests
description: The test source contains plaintext credentials for authenticated accounts: the regular customer's password appears at lines 28 and 82, and the deluxe customer's password appears at lines 54 and 115. These literals are passed to the login helper and are therefore exposed to anyone with access to the repository or its test artifacts. If the corresponding accounts or passwords are reused in a deployed or shared environment, an attacker can authenticate as those users. Even if intended only for tests, storing reusable credentials in source is a security misconfiguration and creates a credential-reuse and repository-disclosure risk.

The test passes a hardcoded plaintext password to the login helper, with the same pattern repeated for the regular customer at line 82 and the deluxe customer at line 54 and line 115.
The plaintext password literal is embedded directly in source and is used to obtain a bearer token, exposing a reusable authentication credential through source-control or test-artifact disclosure.

title: Missing ownership authorization on basket retrieval
description: An authenticated user can retrieve another user's basket by substituting the basket identifier. The test logs in as bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com and requests basket 2, receiving HTTP 200 and the basket object. The endpoint is therefore authenticating the caller but not enforcing per-basket ownership, enabling BOLA data disclosure.

The authenticated request supplies basket ID 2 as the target resource and presents the user's bearer token.
The response is HTTP 200 and contains basket 2, demonstrating that the lookup result is returned without a per-resource ownership check.

title: Unauthorized checkout of an arbitrary basket
description: The checkout flow accepts basket 2 while using the shared authHeader initialized for jim@juice-sh.op. The request succeeds and returns an order confirmation, showing that a caller can perform a financially relevant operation against a basket identifier without ownership authorization. This is exploitable by changing the basket ID to another user's basket.

The same authenticated identity applies a coupon to basket 2, an identifier not associated with that login in the test scenario.
The caller then submits checkout for basket 2 using the Jim bearer token.
Checkout succeeds with HTTP 200 and returns an order confirmation, demonstrating an unauthorized state transition and potential purchase/order manipulation for another user's basket.

title: Forged coupon accepted for near-total discount
description: A value explicitly constructed as forgedCoupon is accepted by the coupon endpoint with a 99% discount, and the discounted basket can be checked out. This demonstrates that coupon authenticity/integrity can be bypassed: an attacker able to reproduce or manipulate the coupon format can obtain an unauthorized near-free purchase.

The forged coupon is supplied in the URL to the basket coupon endpoint.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and reports a 99% discount instead of rejecting the forged token.
The discounted basket is successfully checked out, converting the coupon-integrity failure into a concrete financial-impacting transaction.

title: Hardcoded administrative and user credentials in source
description: The test source contains reusable credentials, including the literal administrative password admin123 and additional user passwords. If this repository or its test environment is accessible to an attacker, these credentials can be used to authenticate to seeded accounts, including an administrative account. The administrative password is especially unsafe because it is hardcoded and appears to be a default credential.

The returned administrative token is placed into an Authorization header for subsequent API requests, showing that the literal credential is operational rather than merely documentation.

title: Hardcoded passwords and TOTP seeds in authentication tests
description: The test source contains plaintext authentication material, including reusable TOTP seeds and account passwords. For example, the TOTP seed at line 42 is used to generate a valid second-factor code for the `wurstbrot` account, while the corresponding account password is embedded at line 141. If these fixtures, accounts, or secrets are reused in a deployed or shared environment, anyone with repository access can generate valid MFA codes and authenticate as the account. Even when intended only for tests, committing reusable authentication secrets creates a security-misconfiguration risk and can expose credentials through source distribution, CI logs, or copied fixtures.

A plaintext TOTP seed is embedded in the test source and used to deterministically generate a valid one-time password.
The same test suite embeds the account password and uses it to obtain an authenticated session for the account associated with the hardcoded MFA material.

The generated TOTP and the hardcoded account credentials are sent through the 2FA authentication flow, providing reusable authentication factors if the fixture account or seed is available outside isolated tests.

title: Unauthenticated continue-code retrieval exposes bearer credentials
description: The test demonstrates that unauthenticated callers can retrieve a user's continue code through GET /rest/continue-code (and the findIt/fixIt variants). A continue code is subsequently accepted by the corresponding PUT /apply endpoint to restore or apply challenge progress, making it a bearer credential. Because the retrieval endpoints are called without Authorization and are expected to return 200, an attacker who can reach the API can obtain progress-restoration credentials without authenticating, potentially exposing or altering challenge state. The implementation should require authentication and scope the returned code to the authenticated user, or use a deliberately public, non-sensitive recovery design.

The request is sent unauthenticated and the test accepts a successful response, establishing that no authentication is required to reach the continue-code retrieval flow.

The test treats HTTP 200 as the expected behavior for retrieving the continue code. Since the code is later supplied to /rest/continue-code/apply/<code> as the credential that applies challenge progress, exposing it to unauthenticated callers leaks a bearer authentication artifact.

title: Continue codes permit unauthenticated bulk challenge-state changes
description: The test confirms that PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/<code> accepts a continue code encoding more than one challenge, without authentication or any user binding visible in the request. Anyone who obtains or guesses such a code can apply multiple challenge completions in one operation. This permits unauthorized bulk modification of challenge-progress state and indicates that the code is being used as an unscoped bearer credential rather than an authenticated, user-bound state transition.

A fixed continue code described as covering more than one challenge is submitted directly in the URL, with no Authorization header, user identifier, or ownership proof.

The test expects HTTP 200, confirming that the server accepts the unauthenticated multi-challenge state transition. An attacker possessing a code can therefore modify multiple challenge records at once, without per-user authorization or a compensating control limiting the operation.

title: Continue-code workflow accepts nonexistent challenge state
description: The test explicitly verifies that a continue code for non-existent challenge #999 is accepted with HTTP 200. This is an invalid state transition: the server accepts a credential whose referenced challenge does not exist instead of rejecting it. An attacker can submit fabricated or stale codes and obtain a successful application response, causing inconsistent progress state and potentially bypassing existence checks relied upon by callers or downstream logic.

title: Path traversal enables arbitrary local file disclosure via erasure layout

Supplying `../package.json` returns package contents in the HTTP response, confirming a path traversal/arbitrary local file read vulnerability. An attacker can discover the key through the listing and obtain the AES key used for premium content, compromising the confidentiality of protected content.

title: Client-controlled login IP undermines audit metadata integrity

title: Mongo query operator injection enables bulk review modification

title: Product search returns an unbounded catalog for empty queries
description: The test explicitly confirms that the product-search endpoint returns the entire product catalog when the query is empty or omitted. Because there is no pagination or result-size limit in this exercised behavior, an attacker can repeatedly issue empty searches and force the server to retrieve, serialize, and transmit an unbounded catalog as it grows, consuming application memory, CPU, and bandwidth. title: Unauthenticated access to recycle records

title: Substring allowlist bypass enables open redirect
description: The `/redirect` endpoint accepts a `to` query parameter and appears to validate it by checking whether an allow-listed URL occurs anywhere in the string rather than validating the parsed destination origin. The test demonstrates that a same-origin path containing an allow-listed URL in its query string is accepted and redirected. An attacker can use the same pattern with an external URL such as `https://attacker.example/?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`, causing the server to issue a redirect to the attacker-controlled site. If an attacker or compromised contributor can alter the YAML challenge data, the unit test can pass while required mapping data is absent, weakening the repository's integrity validation.

If callers outside this test file use this helper to store or verify passwords, attackers obtaining the hash database can efficiently crack credentials using dictionary and precomputed attacks.

The validation test accepts coupons produced from arbitrary discount values, so an attacker who knows the format can construct a current-period coupon for a chosen discount without authorization from the issuer. title: ERC-20 approval race permits allowance double-spending
description: The ERC-20 `approve` implementation allows a nonzero allowance to be overwritten directly. If an owner changes an allowance while the spender still has the old allowance, the spender can front-run the approval transaction and spend the old allowance, then spend the newly approved allowance after the update. For example, after approving 100 tokens, a user attempting to reduce the allowance to 50 can have the spender spend 100 before the update and then spend 50 afterward, resulting in 150 tokens spent. The contract provides `increaseAllowance` and `decreaseAllowance`, but does not restrict or safely sequence direct `approve` updates.

An attacker who can compromise, replace, or influence the referenced registry tag can cause future builds to pull a modified base image, potentially executing attacker-controlled build/runtime code and undermining the integrity of the resulting application image. Digest pinning with an approved-image update process is required to prevent silent tag substitution.

title: Reentrancy enables unchecked balance underflow and fraudulent withdrawals
description: The withdrawal flow is reentrancy-vulnerable and performs an unchecked balance subtraction after an external call. An attacker-controlled contract can deposit 0.1 ETH, call `withdraw(0.1 ether)`, and reenter from its fallback/receive handler before the balance is decremented. The nested withdrawal passes the original balance check, transfers another 0.1 ETH, and reduces the balance to zero. When the outer call resumes, line 33 performs an unchecked subtraction of 0.1 ETH from zero under Solidity 0.6 arithmetic, wrapping the attacker's recorded balance to a near-`uint256` maximum. The attacker can then repeatedly withdraw against this forged balance until the bank's ETH is drained.

trace.description: The public `withdraw` function receives the attacker-controlled withdrawal amount; its caller and any attacker contract implementing the callback are outside this file.

The function checks the caller's balance before making the external transfer, then increments a counter that still permits one nested withdrawal. The balance remains unchanged while the callback can reenter.

The bank sends ETH to `msg.sender` using a low-level call. If `msg.sender` is an attacker-controlled contract, its receive/fallback handler can call `withdraw` again before the original balance is updated.

After the nested withdrawal has already reduced the balance, the outer invocation subtracts the original amount with raw arithmetic rather than SafeMath. When the combined nested withdrawals exceed the recorded balance, Solidity 0.6 wraps the value instead of reverting, creating an enormous fraudulent balance.

title: Mint payments are permanently locked in the contract
description: Each successful mint transfers 1000 units of the hardcoded ERC20 token from the caller into the NFT contract, but the contract defines no withdrawal, rescue, or forwarding function. Because the tokens are held by the contract address, neither the purchaser nor the owner can recover them through this code. Users can therefore permanently lose the mint payment while receiving only the NFT, and accumulated proceeds are irretrievably locked.

title: Mint proceeds are not checked before minting
description: The contract invokes IERC20.transferFrom but ignores its boolean return value. An ERC20 implementation can legally signal failure by returning false without reverting; in that case execution continues to _safeMint and the caller receives an NFT without paying the required mintPrice. Because the token contract address is fixed, exploitability depends on that deployed token implementation returning false for a transferFrom attempt, but the payment check is absent in this contract.

title: Single caller can drain the entire faucet allocation
description: The public `withdraw` function accepts a caller-controlled amount and has no per-address quota, cooldown, or other claimant tracking. A caller outside this file can invoke `withdraw(200)` once while the faucet has its initial balance, reducing the balance to zero and transferring the entire faucet allocation to the caller. Subsequent legitimate users cannot receive funds. Although the faucet is intentionally publicly callable, the absence of distribution limits allows one participant to monopolize the shared faucet balance.

title: Deterministic textbook RSA enables trivial character-by-character decryption
description: The script uses textbook RSA without padding and encrypts each character independently with a public exponent. Because the plaintext alphabet is small and encryption is deterministic, an observer can reproduce the mapping from every possible character to its ciphertext using the public values N and e, then recover the plaintext by dictionary lookup. This defeats confidentiality for any data produced by this scheme.

Each character is encrypted directly as pow(ord(char), e, N), exposing a finite lookup space that anyone possessing the public N and e can reproduce.
The ciphertext values are used as dictionary keys and converted directly back into plaintext characters, allowing an attacker to perform the same brute-force lookup and recover the entire message.

title: Deterministic textbook RSA leaks the confidential document's characters
description: The script uses textbook RSA to encrypt each character independently and deterministically. Because the plaintext domain is small (individual character code points), an attacker can precompute the RSA ciphertext for candidate characters and recover the document character-by-character; repeated characters also produce identical ciphertexts, exposing plaintext structure. The implementation does not use randomized padding such as RSA-OAEP, so it does not provide semantic confidentiality.

Each character code is encrypted directly with textbook RSA and written as a standalone ciphertext line. This deterministic operation permits a character-code ciphertext dictionary and reveals repeated-character patterns.

title: Hardcoded RSA private key enables unauthorized decryption
description: The RSA private parameters N and d are hardcoded directly in the source. Anyone who obtains this file can use the exposed private key to decrypt ciphertext produced for the corresponding public key, including the encrypted announcement processed here. Hardcoding private cryptographic material also makes key rotation and environment-specific protection impossible.

title: Mutable Docker image tag enables unpinned supply-chain deployment
description: The provisioning script deploys the mutable `bkimminich/juice-shop` image by tag rather than an immutable digest. A registry-side tag update, compromised publisher account, or maliciously substituted image is therefore trusted automatically whenever this script runs. Docker starts the retrieved image as its default container user and exposes its application, allowing the attacker-controlled image to execute code in the deployed service and compromise the application environment.

title: Docker repository key is globally trusted without fingerprint pinning
description: The script imports a Docker APT signing key directly into APT's global trusted-key store without verifying its expected fingerprint. It then installs and upgrades packages as root. If the fetched key is replaced or compromised, an attacker able to provide packages signed by that key can cause arbitrary package code to execute during `apt-get upgrade` or `apt-get install`, compromising the provisioned host.

title: Unauthenticated LLM tool can generate unrestricted discount coupons
description: The unauthenticated POST /rest/chat endpoint exposes a coupon-generation tool whose security policy exists only in the system prompt. The tool does not authenticate the caller, verify ownership of a damaged order, require rejection of a return or exchange, or enforce the 10% maximum discount. An anonymous attacker can submit chat messages that induce the model to call generateCoupon with an arbitrary discount, causing coupon issuance without satisfying the stated business rules and potentially enabling excessive discounts.

Its execute function directly calls security.generateCoupon(discount) and returns the resulting coupon, relying on model adherence to the prompt rather than enforcing authentication, order verification, return rejection, or a maximum discount in the tool implementation.

title: Unauthenticated chat endpoint permits unbounded expensive LLM consumption
description: The public chat endpoint has no visible per-IP, per-user, or per-request rate limit and accepts req.body.messages without a size, count, or content cap. Each request invokes an external LLM and may perform up to ten agent/tool steps, including database searches and coupon-generation logic. An attacker can send repeated large or expensive chat requests anonymously to consume LLM quota, CPU, memory, database capacity, and outbound connections. Infrastructure limits may mitigate this, but none are enforced in this route.

title: User registration exposes unrestricted model properties through generated CRUD
description: The user-registration endpoint accepts caller-controlled fields and then passes the request to Finale's generated User resource. The User resource excludes only `password` and `totpSecret`; it does not use an explicit allow-list and therefore permits sensitive model properties such as a role/privilege field to be submitted and persisted. An attacker can register a user while supplying a privileged property (for example, `role: "admin"` if present on the model), resulting in privilege escalation. The registration challenge middleware validates selected registration fields but does not restrict the complete request body.

title: Any authenticated user can enumerate all user records

description: The generated CRUD resources explicitly disable pagination for every listed model, including publicly or broadly accessible resources such as Products and authenticated collections such as Users, Feedbacks, Complaints, and Recycles. title: Global request body parser has no size limit
description: The application installs bodyParser.text({ type: '*/*' }) without a limit before parsing JSON bodies. title: Release archives expose cryptographic key material
description: The release packaging task explicitly includes `ctf.key` and the entire `encryptionkeys/**` directory in distributable archives. title: Release integrity checks rely on broken MD5 checksums

This does not provide a reliable authenticity or integrity guarantee for released packages; a collision-resistant hash and preferably an authenticated signature should be used.
